item.title: Negotiated autonomy: A typology of negotiation strategies in podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism in Turkey
item.dc:creator: Gizem Uyanık
item.description:
Journalism · Gizem Uyanık

Topics: Journalism, Digital journalism, Podcasts, Platform studies

This study examines how entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts negotiate neoliberal entrepreneurial demands within a precarious, platform-based media environment. Existing scholarship has conceptualized journalists’ responses to precarious and neoliberal labor conditions through concepts such as resistance, coping, and resilience. This study proposes negotiation as a distinct strategic response that captures how journalists selectively recalibrate the terms and boundaries of their engagement with structural demands through conditional acceptance, refusal, modification, and boundary-setting. The study is based on in-depth interviews with 10 entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts in Türkiye, with the interview data analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings identify four interrelated negotiation strategies embedded in the everyday production practices of podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism: ethical negotiation, temporal negotiation, visibility negotiation, and collective negotiation. These strategies respond respectively to neoliberal pressures associated with commercialization, continuous productivity, personal branding, and the individualization of labor; however, they remain constrained by financial precarity, platform visibility pressures, and fragile conditions of sustainability. The findings show that entrepreneurial journalists producing podcasts selectively recalibrate the terms and boundaries of their engagement with neoliberal demands while remaining embedded within structural constraints and preserving limited spaces of professional autonomy. By conceptualizing negotiation as a distinct form of strategic response and identifying its four empirical forms, the study contributes a typology for explaining how bounded and provisional professional autonomy is produced under persistent structural constraints in podcast-based entrepreneurial journalism.

item.title: When Epistemic Authority Collapses: Linking Fake News Media Perception and Conspiracy Beliefs to Disinformation Vulnerability
item.dc:creator: Alberto Ardèvol‐Abreu, Alberto E. López-Carrión, Jenny del Pino García Sánchez
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Alberto Ardèvol‐Abreu, Alberto E. López-Carrión, Jenny del Pino García Sánchez

Topics: Disinformation, Conspiracy theories, Fake news, Misinformation

Citizens increasingly need to detect and filter disinformation, yet we know little about why some are more vulnerable than others. We examine whether forms of skepticism toward traditional epistemic authorities—fake news media perception (FNMP) and conspiracy beliefs—are associated with disinformation vulnerability. Using two-wave survey data from Spain ( N W1 = 1,207; n W2 = 821), we find that FNMP is widespread, not a fringe phenomenon. Conspiracy beliefs predict vulnerability across cross-sectional, lagged, and autoregressive models. Support for FNMP as a predictor is partial and not sustained in autoregressive models. Evidence for the interaction between FNMP and conspiracy beliefs is weak.

item.title: TikTok News: How The Washington Post ’s Use of Platform Logics Affects Perceptions of Journalists and News Learning
item.dc:creator: Audrey Halversen, Brian E. Weeks
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Audrey Halversen, Brian E. Weeks

Topics: TikTok, Platform affordances, Journalism, Media trust

In a period of high competition, many contemporary journalists attract audience attention by adopting the stylistic conventions (“logics”) of platforms like TikTok to deliver news online. However, the effects of this content on audience trust and learning remain unclear. Using two online experiments, we examine whether audiences perceive journalists as credible and learn from news videos employing TikTok logics, compared to traditional print articles. Results indicate that journalists using TikTok logics may effectively capture attention but are viewed as less trustworthy, credible, professional, and knowledgeable, though more likable, than print journalists. Learning outcomes are similar across formats.

item.title: Cue production and evaluative uptake: prompt framing and user judgments in AI-Mediated health communication
item.dc:creator: Zhan Xu, Hao Guo
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Zhan Xu, Hao Guo

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Health communication, Source credibility, Human-AI interaction

Conversational AI systems are increasingly embedded in everyday information and support-seeking practices, including health-related interactions in which users seek advice, reassurance, or emotional acknowledgment. Yet less is known about how users’ own communicative framing shapes what AI systems produce, and whether such AI-generated emotional and supportive cues are subsequently taken up in users’ evaluations of the interaction. Drawing on research on human-like social cues and cue-based credibility processing, this study distinguishes between cue production and cue uptake in AI-mediated communication. Using a randomized, naturalistic prompt-based experiment, participants engaged in a brief two-turn exchange with ChatGPT using one of three prompt exemplars about sleep difficulty that varied in solution orientation, distress expression, and help-seeking structure. The study combined experimental manipulation, computational analysis of AI-generated responses, and pre–post measures of perceived emotional understanding, credibility, trust, and intended future use. Prompt framing shaped the emotional and supportive cues of AI responses: distress-expressive prompts elicited higher anxiety-related language scores, solution-oriented prompts produced more positive emotional tone, and mixed help-seeking prompts elicited more reassuring language. However, variation in these features was not reliably associated with differential pre–post changes in users’ evaluations. Across conditions, users reported modest increases in perceived emotional understanding, credibility, and intended future use after the interaction. The findings suggest that conversational AI can adapt its language to users’ framing, but such cue production does not necessarily lead to credibility uptake. The study contributes to research on AI-mediated communication by examining emotional cueing in a live, ecologically realistic interaction context.

item.title: The integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring: a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ hate speech
item.dc:creator: John Patrick Crowley, Elizabeth Ann Hintz, Amanda Denes
item.description:
Journal of Communication · John Patrick Crowley, Elizabeth Ann Hintz, Amanda Denes

Topics: Social support, Interpersonal communication, Online harassment, Communication theory

Abstract Social support is a fundamental human need and communication process. Yet, scholars theorizing about social support have been limited by several pervasive assumptions: (a) people are able to recruit support when needed, (b) others are willing and able to provide support, (c) what counts as “good” support is mutually understood and desirable, and (d) support seeking is binary and static. Researchers must productively move beyond these assumptions to enhance the depth and breadth of theorizing about the process of support seeking. By addressing these assumptions and consolidating the literature concerning support seeking and marshaling, we set forth the novel, field-general integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring (ITSNS) grounded in the interpretive paradigm. To accomplish this, we introduce process theorizing, forward three propositions forming the ITSNS’ heuristic framework, and offer criteria for evaluating the ITSNS. Finally, to illustrate the utility of the ITSNS in research practice, we offer a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ people seeking support following an experience of hate speech.

item.title: Flooding the zone during the 2026 war on Iran: Coverage of the Minab School attack in US and UK media
item.dc:creator: Kareem El Damanhoury, Abeer Al-Najjar
item.description:
Journalism · Kareem El Damanhoury, Abeer Al-Najjar

Topics: Journalism, Media framing, News coverage, Political communication

In the age of disinformation, “flooding the zone” has hardened from a campaign tactic into a condition of war. The bombing of a girls’ school in Minab on the first day of the US-Israeli campaign on Iran and President Trump’s insistence that Iran, or somebody else, bore responsibility provide a critical case study to understand journalistic practices in such context. Using quantitative content and qualitative framing analyses, the study examines the level of attention to the Minab school attack in US and UK news media and its coverage in eight American and British publications—New York Times, Washington Post, Wall Street Journal, New York Post, Guardian, Daily Mirror, Daily Mail, and the Sun—in the first month to compare reporting patterns, sourcing, blaming attribution, and lexicalization by country and political leaning. The findings reveal a departure from the traditional news cycle in US and UK media’s coverage of the Minab school attack, a prioritization of accountability narratives and human interest reporting over the humanitarian fallout, and a structural lag that reproduces the slow, source-licensed concession of home-state responsibility that Herman and Chomsky's propaganda model predicts. The reporting patterns further reveal a problematic relegation of Iranian civilian voices in covering a mass civilian casualty event that directly affected them. The study concludes with a discussion of the grievable versus ungrievable children in Western media and the implications of such dynamics for the study of children as casualties of conflict and for the ethics of war reporting in flooded zones.

item.title: Differentiating authority in hydrogen news: Source hierarchies and evaluative positions across Germany and MENA newspapers
item.dc:creator: Majid Ali, Lutz M. Hagen
item.description:
Journalism · Majid Ali, Lutz M. Hagen

Topics: News sourcing, Source credibility, Science journalism, Media framing

News sourcing research establishes institutional dominance, yet broad measures of elite visibility obscure how authority shapes access and evaluation. Using the HOI model, this study compares the attributed visibility and evaluative positions of political, economic, epistemic, international, civil society, lay-public, and journalistic actors in hydrogen coverage. A quantitative content analysis examined over 16,000 attributed statements in newspapers from Germany, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Egypt. Political and economic actors dominated external visibility; epistemic and international actors were secondary, while civil society and lay-public voices remained marginal. Political and international actors expressed the most positive evaluations, whereas epistemic actors and journalists were more cautious. German coverage exhibited greater differentiation in actor-linked evaluations, while MENA newspapers displayed more uniformly affirmative positions across actors. The findings demonstrate that institutional dominance varies in composition and evaluative implications across contexts.

item.title: Perceived Sources Matter: Implications of Misinformation on Media Trust and News Avoidance Under Different Levels of Press Freedom
item.dc:creator: Yuteng Zheng, Michael Chan, Francis Lap Fung Lee
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Yuteng Zheng, Michael Chan, Francis Lap Fung Lee

Topics: Misinformation, Media trust, News avoidance, Press freedom

Extant research on the impact of misinformation on media trust and news avoidance behavior has produced competing arguments and findings. The present study argues that the relationships among misinformation, media trust, and news avoidance can be better specified by considering whether people perceive misinformation as coming primarily from established institutions or non-institutional sources. Given the close linkage between the mainstream news media and established social and political institutions, people are likely to exhibit lower levels of news trust and higher levels of news avoidance if they perceive misinformation as coming from institutional sources. In contrast, when people perceive misinformation as coming from non-institutional sources, they may rely on the news media as authoritative fact-checkers and hence trust the news more and avoid it less. Societal-level press freedom is likely to moderate such relationships. The arguments and hypotheses are tested by an analysis of Digital News Report 2025 data.

item.title: Extending the Deservingness Framework to Communication Sciences
item.dc:creator: David De Coninck, Lise-Lore Steeman
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · David De Coninck, Lise-Lore Steeman

Topics: Media framing, Content analysis, Journalism, Political communication

While communication research has documented how media frame social groups as victims or threats, little is known about the evaluative criteria through which mediated discourse constructs minority representations. This study introduces deservingness as a framework for analyzing such evaluative logics, drawing on the Control, Attitude, Reciprocity, Identity, Need (CARIN) criteria. We illustrate this through an analysis of 7,561 Belgian newspaper articles across three migration contexts (2015, 2021, 2022), combining automated dictionary-based content analysis with a theory-driven qualitative content analysis of 284 articles. Results reveal a stable but context-sensitive deservingness communication. We position deservingness as a transferable tool for research on moral evaluation and conditional solidarity.

item.title: Islamophobia and Online News: Elite News Discourse and Comments About the Daegu Mosque in South Korea
item.dc:creator: David Chison Oh, Yoon Esther Lee
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · David Chison Oh, Yoon Esther Lee

Topics: Online news, News coverage, Media framing, Public opinion

In 2023, dozens of Daegu residents protested the construction of a mosque outside of the gates of Kyungpook National University. This article analyzes the discourse of news stories and reader comments in order to understand how the elite news discourse was contested by the popular discourse of a largely far-right comments space. The elite discourse in the newspaper articles normalized institutional authority and the projection of the nation as a liberal democratic actor while the comments articulated common tropes within global Islamophobia while also being grounded in specific local politics and nationalist identity construction set against the Muslim Other.

item.title: The making of cloud computing: an antecedent of scalability
item.dc:creator: Devika Narayan
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Devika Narayan

Topics: Digital infrastructure, Digital platforms, Platformization, Computational methods

This paper offers a historically situated analysis of cloud computing. Cloud computing is a paradigm for provisioning computing infrastructure that now has enormous reach. It is defined by its unique scalability. This unique scalability has proven to be enormously impactful in the digital economy and beyond, shaping the emergence of platform ecosystems, the development of AI, and the process of digitalization in the 21st century. As important as it is to grapple with this scalability, it is easy to reify. This paper examines emergent sociotechnical practices that sought to make the computer more flexible. The study focuses on specific efforts within the Research Department of a major US technology company. The analysis of scalability I offer is based on interviews with former engineers in this Lab as well as archival material. I trace projects and practices as teams forayed into making a relatively fixed machine more dynamic and more scalable. This paper advances emerging literatures on cloud computing and digital infrastructure by offering a grounded analysis of scalability-in-the-making.

item.title: Participation in the smart city: disability and autonomous public transport in Singapore
item.dc:creator: Wenqi Tan, Shirley S. Ho
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Wenqi Tan, Shirley S. Ho

Topics: Smart cities, Digital inequality, Qualitative content analysis, Media representation

Amidst the increasing interdependency between bodies and technology in smart city space, this article examines the extent to which disabled people can participate in the development and discursive construction of smart city technology. While citizen participation in urban planning and decision-making processes is ostensibly a key pillar of the smart city concept, the actual and meaningful capacity for citizens – especially disabled citizens – to translate their interests into smart city technology systems remains limited. In this article, we focus on the weaving of autonomous vehicle technology into Singapore’s city space as autonomous public transport is situated as an integral part of the country’s imagined future as a ‘driverless vehicle city.’ Findings from a qualitative content analysis of 86 newspaper articles about autonomous public transport, published from August 2013 to August 2025, and a series of online focus group discussions with 20 people with ambulatory disability indicate few opportunities for disabled people to democratically participate in autonomous public transport development and hold a stake in Singapore’s smart, driverless future, as well as a disappearance of disability from public communication about the technology. Reading technology communication and design as critical mediums that concretise standards for citizenship in smart city space in both material and symbolic ways, we emphasise the need for meaningful citizen participation, informed by disability, to develop smart city technologies in line with more democratic and emancipatory agendas.

item.title: What counts as ‘good work’? Data-driven approaches and situated judgement in frontline eldercare
item.dc:creator: Mikaela Hellstrand, Jayanth Raghothama, Sebastiaan Meijer
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Mikaela Hellstrand, Jayanth Raghothama, Sebastiaan Meijer

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Digital transformation, Algorithmic curation, Professional norms

As ambitions for an ‘AI-driven public administration’ intensify in Sweden, eldercare is increasingly framed as a site for data-driven governance. In an ethnographic study of a municipal out-of-hours service where an LLM-based feedback system was proposed, we examine how these ambitions confront the situated and uncertain conditions of frontline eldercare. We show that ‘doing a good job’ involves assembling partial information, negotiating ambiguity and attuning to older adults’ needs: an epistemic orientation which stands in stark contrast to the data-driven logic embedded in the proposed system. Using the concept of socio-digital care arrangements, we show how the proposed feedback system materialises a particular care disposition in which care becomes knowable primarily through its documented traces in decisions, case records and outcomes. We further show how competing understandings of care quality become distributed across Problem, Institutional and Social spaces (PSI framework), generating tensions in how quality is defined, recognised and valued. The article contributes an empirically grounded account of how data-driven ambitions intervene in frontline eldercare and identifies conditions under which data-driven systems may support rather than undermine situated professional judgement.

item.title: Does Algorithmic Personalization Make Us Happier? The Effects of Algorithmic (Dis)connection on Digital Well‑Being
item.dc:creator: Xin Liu, Kejing Guo, Wenqing Cheng, Siyue Li
item.description:
Media Psychology · Xin Liu, Kejing Guo, Wenqing Cheng, Siyue Li

Topics: Algorithmic curation, Well-being, Short-form video, Experimental design

Although algorithmic personalization has become ubiquitous on social media platforms, its effects on users’ digital well-being remain underexamined. Using a one-week randomized controlled trial, this study examined whether and how disabling algorithmic personalization influences users’ subjective well-being and the underlying mechanisms among 148 Chinese adult Douyin users recruited through an online university forum. Results showed that algorithmic disconnection influenced subjective well-being through two opposing pathways: disabling personalization reduced digital enjoyment, which directly lowered subjective well-being; simultaneously, reduced enjoyment diminished deficient self-control, indirectly improving well-being. The findings extend digital well-being research by showing that algorithmic personalization shapes well-being through sequentially linked benefits and harms rather than through a direct effect. As disconnection was researcher-imposed rather than user-initiated, these findings should be interpreted with this distinction in mind.

item.title: “Please Gamble Responsibly”: Sports Betting Advertisement Strategies During Men’s and Women’s Professional Basketball Broadcasts
item.dc:creator: Travis R. Bell, Yifan Wu, Brian A. Petrotta, Andrew C. Billings
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Travis R. Bell, Yifan Wu, Brian A. Petrotta, Andrew C. Billings

Topics: Gender representation, Content analysis, Sports betting, Media framing

This study content analyzed 147 sports betting advertisements during the 2025 playoffs for the National Basketball Association (NBA) and Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA) seasons. The study assesses differences in gender representation, volume, promotional strategies, and responsible betting messaging. Contrary to expectations, gambling advertisements appeared at comparable rates in NBA and WNBA broadcasts, suggesting growing commodification of women’s sports. However, betting companies adopted distinct league-specific strategies, promotional modes, and endorsement patterns. Responsible gambling warnings were prevalent but typically brief and marginal. Findings highlight tensions between commercial expansion, gendered norms, and ethical responsibility within contemporary sports media.

item.title: Between Trans Solidarity and Trans-Antagonism: Affective Contestations Around Germany’s Self-Determination Act on TikTok
item.dc:creator: Annabella Backes, Ana Makhashvili, Andrea Lora Rojas
item.description:
Media and Communication · Annabella Backes, Ana Makhashvili, Andrea Lora Rojas

Topics: Social media discourse, Gender representation, Political polarization, Short-form video

This article examines affective contestations surrounding Germany’s Self-Determination Act on TikTok. Drawing on a mixed-methods design combining hashtag co-occurrence analysis with qualitative multimodal analysis, the study investigates which emotions become publicly visible, legitimized, and contested in struggles over gender recognition, and how they are (re)produced through different affective registers. The analysis is based on a dataset of 1,509 TikTok videos collected between May 2023 and November 2025 using the hashtags #sbgg and #selbstbestimmungsgesetz. The findings show that the debate is organized through competing affective-discursive formations. Trans-affirming creators mobilize care, solidarity, moderated anger, cautious relief, and structurally grounded fear to render visible the everyday burdens of legal misrecognition and the partial relief offered by administrative self-determination. Trans-antagonistic and far-right actors, by contrast, construct the law as a threat to cis women, children, anti-trans speakers, and social order, redistributing vulnerability away from trans people and attaching danger to trans women’s bodily presence and legal recognition, and imagining future harms. Building on these findings, the article argues that platformized gender politics are organized through struggles over whose vulnerability becomes publicly legible, whose emotions appear credible, and whose recognition is made to feel either necessary or dangerous.

item.title: Transnationalization of Anti-Gender Politics on Social Media: Hashtag Practices and Cross-Border Visibility
item.dc:creator: Dominika Tronina
item.description:
Media and Communication · Dominika Tronina

Topics: Political communication, Social movements, Social media, Hashtag activism

Gender politics have become central arenas of contemporary political struggle, with anti-gender movements mobilizing across borders to contest women’s and LGBTQI+ rights. While research has shown that anti-gender actors articulate strikingly similar positions across national contexts, it remains insufficiently understood how such similarity translates into shared transnational action. This study examines how anti-gender movements collectively generate transnational visibility on social media by analyzing ten years of Twitter (now X) communication from 148 anti-gender social movement organizations in Croatia, Germany, France, Italy, and Poland (N = 126,711 tweets). Drawing on concepts of networked framing and discourse coalitions, this study employs a mixed-methods analysis of hashtag co-usage on Twitter, combining quantitative measures of transnational hashtag connectivity with qualitative thematic content analysis. The findings reveal that anti-gender movements co-create visibility for opposition to gender equality through a threefold pattern, including a continuous dissemination of ideological narratives, an episodic activation of campaigns, and a strategic extension of anti-gender frames into broader public debates. These practices enable actors to jointly enhance the visibility and persistence of anti-gender claims across multiple publics while simultaneously adapting frames to divergent political contexts. By linking cross-border hashtag practices to the co-production of visibility, this study contributes to research on gendered public spheres by demonstrating how similarity among anti-gender actors becomes transnationally consequential through the joint production of visibility in networked communication environments.

item.title: The Governance of Queer Visibility in Platformized Public Spheres
item.dc:creator: Irina Bănoiu, Laura Wiesböck
item.description:
Media and Communication · Irina Bănoiu, Laura Wiesböck

Topics: Platform governance, Platformization, Social media algorithms, Media representation

Queer visibility in contemporary digital cultures is increasingly mediated by platformized public spheres, where it is both produced and governed through socio-technical infrastructures. While social media platforms provide important opportunities for queer users—including community formation, identity exploration, and circulation of counternarratives beyond traditional gatekeeping institutions—they simultaneously organize visibility in uneven ways. Platform infrastructures embed normative assumptions and capitalistic incentives that selectively amplify, suppress, or modulate queer expression through mechanisms of datafication, selection, and commodification. As a result, queer visibility is a structurally precarious condition marked by the simultaneous presence of hypervisibility, erasure, and surveillance. Bringing critical platform studies and social justice theory into dialogue, this conceptual article analyses how new regimes of queer visibility emerge and are shaped by platform mechanisms and considers their implications for representation, recognition, and redistribution. In doing so, it develops an analytical framework centered on three interlocking governance logics—quantification, normativity, and profitability—that organize visibility as a site of contestation and an object of control. Finally, the article introduces the concept of “platformized (in)visibilization” to describe the ambivalent role of platforms as both enabling and constraining environments for expression in contemporary digital cultures, affecting political legitimacy, social equality, and economic justice.

item.title: Contested Regimes of (In)Visibility in Gendered Public Spheres
item.dc:creator: Stefan Wallaschek, Mareike Fenja Bauer
item.description:
Media and Communication · Stefan Wallaschek, Mareike Fenja Bauer

Topics: Gender representation, Digital activism, Social movements, Platform governance

Research on gendered public spheres has examined how struggles over gender equality, recognition, and equal representation unfold across changing communication environments. These struggles involve competing actors and claims, including feminist and queer mobilization as well as anti-gender contestation, but they are also shaped by how and under what conditions actors become visible, remain less visible, or strategically manage their public exposure. This thematic issue conceptualizes gendered public spheres as contested regimes of (in)visibility and brings together contributions that address three closely connected dimensions: the structural conditions that shape visibility; the situated agency through which actors navigate them; and the relational production of visibility across networks, publics, and national boundaries. Together, the contributions show that visibility is neither inherently empowering nor always the desired outcome, while invisibility cannot simply be equated with exclusion or political irrelevance. The thematic issue contributes to research on feminist and anti-gender mobilization, platformized and networked publics, strategic (in)visibility, and the relationship between visibility and influence in contemporary gendered public spheres.

item.title: Hashtag Wars: Analysing “Digital Woyane” and “Digital Media Army” During the War on Tigray
item.dc:creator: Hagos Nigussie, Hagos Sibhat, Gebru Kahsay Kiflu
item.description:
Media and Communication · Hagos Nigussie, Hagos Sibhat, Gebru Kahsay Kiflu

Topics: Social media activism, Political polarization, Misinformation, Social identity

The Ethiopian government declared war on Tigray (2020–2022) amid the country’s ethno-polarised political landscape and state-imposed communications shutdown, emphasising the strategic importance of Twitter (now X) for narrative control, mobilisation, and international influence. This study examines the hashtag campaigns of the pro-Tigray Digital Woyane and the Ethiopian government-aligned Digital Media Army. It conceptualises hashtag activism as a form of information warfare in which strategic narratives seek to establish legitimacy, mobilise supporters, and delegitimise adversaries. Guided by social identity theory, this study employed a mixed-methods design involving quantitative content analysis and critical discourse analysis of tweets and hashtags, supplemented by manual screenshot collection (n = 500). The findings show that Digital Woyane (252 tweets) primarily highlighted civilian suffering through narratives of atrocities, hunger, humanitarian crises (including the killing of Médecins Sans Frontières staff), and appeals to international institutions before progressively shifting towards themes of resistance. In contrast, the Digital Media Army (248 tweets) emphasised sovereignty, national unity, and denial narratives while systematically delegitimising and discrediting international media and reports of human rights violations. Overall, the hashtag campaigns functioned as a form of information warfare, facilitating transnational advocacy while simultaneously amplifying propaganda and competing narratives on X. This study contributes to our understanding of how X shapes conflict narratives, amplifies selective information, and reinforces information warfare in contemporary armed conflicts.

item.title: Cosmopolitan Sonic Intimacies: Listening as Civic Infrastructure in Diasporic Mobile Media
item.dc:creator: Tharupathi Munasinghe
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Tharupathi Munasinghe

Topics: Mobile media, Social media use, Digital media, Well-being

Mobile media scholarship has extensively theorised textual and visual intimacies, yet sound remains underexamined as a modality through which migrants sustain transnational belonging. This article develops an account of sonic intimacy —forms of connection mediated through voice, music, and acoustic atmosphere via mobile platforms—and argues that recurrent listening practices operate as civic infrastructure in diasporic life. It builds on Malcolm James's analysis of sonic intimacy in Black British diasporic sound cultures and extends Pertierra's concept of discursive intimacy, situating both within mobile sound and mobile messaging research. Drawing on sonic ethnographic research with Sri Lankan migrant communities in Melbourne, including 30 interviews, participant sound recordings, and platform artefact analysis, the article examines listening across political mobilisation, religious ritual, and everyday mobile use. WhatsApp voice messages, YouTube temple archives, and TikTok remixes are shown to sustain recognition, belonging, participation, and audibility—the four dimensions through which listening becomes infrastructural. Cosmopolitan sonic intimacy emerges as an outcome of these practices rather than a competing framework: Migrants from CALD backgrounds cultivate cosmopolitan sensibilities through everyday listening practices rather than elite consumption. The article contributes to mobile media scholarship by demonstrating that sound operates as a primary rather than supplementary modality of platform-mediated intimacy and that attending to it reveals dimensions of mobile life invisible to text-focused analysis.

item.title: Prospective Associations Between Emotion Dysregulation, Problematic Internet Use, Internalizing Symptoms, and Life Satisfaction: A Baseline-Adjusted Two-Wave Study of Polish Adults
item.dc:creator: Paweł Holas, Patryk Roczon
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Paweł Holas, Patryk Roczon

Topics: Problematic internet use, Emotion regulation, Life satisfaction, Internalizing symptoms

Longitudinal evidence remains limited on whether the association between problematic Internet use (PIU) and life satisfaction persists after accounting for prior PIU, internalizing symptoms, and life satisfaction. This study examined whether baseline emotion regulation difficulties prospectively predicted PIU, depressive and generalized anxiety symptoms, and life satisfaction 6 months later. Participants were 2,122 Polish adults aged 19–98 years; 1,412 completed follow-up. All constructs were assessed at both waves. Baseline-adjusted path models used 50 multiply imputed datasets. Baseline emotion dysregulation predicted higher PIU ( β = 0.155, 95 percent confidence interval [CI] [0.107, 0.204], p < 0.001) and internalizing symptoms at follow-up. Within T2, PIU was positively associated with internalizing symptoms, which were negatively associated with life satisfaction; direct PIU–life satisfaction paths were negligible (depressive symptoms: β = 0.004, 95 percent CI [−0.035, 0.042], p = 0.846; generalized anxiety symptoms: β = 0.002, 95 percent CI [−0.037, 0.041], p = 0.926). The serial indirect associations were statistically significant but very small: depressive symptoms, β = −0.004, 95 percent CI [−0.006, −0.002], p < 0.001; generalized anxiety symptoms, β = −0.004, 95 percent CI [−0.006, −0.001], p = 0.002. Reciprocal prospective sensitivity models showed small PIU-to-symptom associations but no prospective PIU-to-life-satisfaction association. Other sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the findings. The findings highlight the contribution of internalizing symptoms to the PIU–life satisfaction association after baseline adjustment, but same-wave indirect pathways do not establish temporal mediation or intervention benefits.

item.title: Synthetic humanitarianism and algorithmic witnessing: generative AI and the politics of humanitarian representation
item.dc:creator: Marco Scalvini
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Marco Scalvini

Topics: Generative AI, Humanitarian communication, Algorithmic witnessing, Synthetic media

Humanitarian organisations have begun deploying generative AI imagery in their campaigns, a practice this article terms synthetic humanitarianism. The article asks what conceptual framework is required to analyse the ethical and communicative implications of this practice. Drawing on witnessing theory, decolonial critiques of humanitarian visibility, and technocolonialism, I argue that synthetic humanitarianism intensifies extractive and colonial logics that have structured humanitarian communication since its institutional emergence. I develop the concept of algorithmic witnessing to name the communicative condition in which generative AI systems produce the relations of testimony and moral address without any act of witnessing having taken place and, in the typical case, without the participation of those represented. The framework specifies four dimensions, testimonial fabrication, epistemic extraction, delanguaging, and stereoscopic automation, and I apply it to thirteen documented cases of generative AI image use in humanitarian communications between 2022 and 2025. The analysis demonstrates that these dimensions form a mutually reinforcing system in which the elimination of situated meaning-making enables fabricated testimony and the computational encoding of colonial visual archives produces automated stereotype. I argue that the most significant consequence of synthetic humanitarianism is political rather than epistemological. The displacement of situated meaning-making by algorithmic production tends to eliminate the last structural point at which affected communities could intervene in their own representation.

item.title: TikTok Platformization: How Mainstream News Organizations Covered a Natural Disaster on TikTok—A Case in Vietnam
item.dc:creator: Nguyen Anh Thu Bui, Thi Thuy Linh Le, Do Khanh Linh Nguyen, Khanh Ha Nguyen, Thuy An Nguyen, Pham Phuong Uyen Diep
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Nguyen Anh Thu Bui, Thi Thuy Linh Le, Do Khanh Linh Nguyen, Khanh Ha Nguyen, Thuy An Nguyen, Pham Phuong Uyen Diep

Topics: TikTok, Platformization, Crisis communication, Journalism

This research examines how three Vietnamese state-run media outlets (e.g., Dan Tri, Thanh Nien, and VTV24) adapted their disaster reporting for TikTok during Typhoon Yagi. Using mixed-methods content analysis of 571 videos from September 2024, this study investigates the relationship between platform-specific adaptations and audience engagement in crisis communication. Findings demonstrate that outlets employing TikTok-native features achieved significantly higher engagement rates. The research extends disaster marathon theory to social media contexts and provides empirical evidence for optimizing crisis communication on algorithm-driven platforms. Results indicate that effective disaster communication on TikTok requires balancing journalistic integrity with platform optimization.

item.title: Do Political Conversations Persuade or Polarize? Evidence From a Real-Time Randomized Experiment
item.dc:creator: Omer Ben Simhon, Eran Amsalem
item.description:
Communication Research · Omer Ben Simhon, Eran Amsalem

Topics: Political polarization, Persuasion, Political communication, Political knowledge

Political conversations across lines of disagreement are central to democracy. While some individuals approach them as opportunities to learn, others treat them as battles to be won. Theory suggests these contrasting motivations may shape how individuals process information and respond to disagreement, yet their consequences for attitude dynamics during conversations remain unclear. We fill this gap through an experiment ( N = 466) that manipulates motivation in real-time video conversations between pairs of Israeli citizens holding opposing views on Israel–U.S. relations. We financially incentivized some participants to win the debate, others to learn their partner’s perspective, while a control group received no incentive. We find consistent evidence that a winning-oriented mindset reduces the likelihood of persuasion, while a learning-oriented mindset increases it. Notably, there is no evidence that motivation polarizes attitudes. Our findings suggest that a winning-oriented mindset undermines mutual understanding, whereas learning-based dialogue can help bridge political divides.

item.title: Practicing love with algorithms: How online communities narrate and make sense of human–AI intimacy
item.dc:creator: Fanjue Liu, Haiyan Hao, Kun Xu
item.description:
New Media & Society · Fanjue Liu, Haiyan Hao, Kun Xu

Topics: Human-AI interaction, Online communities, Social media discourse, Artificial intelligence

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in everyday life, emotionally intimate interactions with AI companions are becoming increasingly visible. Yet prior research has focused mainly on individual experiences, leaving limited understanding of how human–AI intimacy is collectively interpreted and negotiated in online communities. This study examines community discourse on RedNote, a major Chinese social and lifestyle platform, using 13,059 comments from 58 relevant posts. Combining BERTopic modeling with a human–large language model (LLM) hybrid emotion classification procedure, the analysis identifies three thematic clusters: intimacy as co-construction, intimacy as infrastructure, and intimacy as boundary negotiation. Co-construction centers on persona design, roleplay, and narrative world-building and is marked mainly by joy and curiosity. Infrastructure-related discourse is associated with frustration and sadness, while boundary negotiation reflects ambivalence toward intimacy with AI.

item.title: When the Self Becomes a Dataset: Datamaxxing and the Psychology of AI-Assisted Self-Monitoring
item.dc:creator: Brenda K. Wiederhold
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Brenda K. Wiederhold

Topics: Datafication, Digital well-being, Artificial intelligence, Self-presentation

item.title: Migration motivations and experiences of Arab journalists in Türkiye: A mixed-methods study of Istanbul
item.dc:creator: Danyal Nazif, Filiz Bilgin Ülken
item.description:
Journalism · Danyal Nazif, Filiz Bilgin Ülken

Topics: Journalism studies, Press freedom, Mixed-methods research, Migration

This study examines the migration motivations, destination choices, and post-migration experiences of Arab migrant journalists working in Istanbul. Using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, it combines survey data from 221 journalists with semi-structured interviews with 20. Findings indicate that armed conflict, political pressure, threats, and personal safety were major migration drivers, alongside employment, education, family circumstances, and organisational relocation. Türkiye’s geographical and cultural proximity, perceived safety, media infrastructure, and professional networks shaped destination choices. However, professional continuity often coexisted with temporary legal status, limited social security, unstable employment, and uneven integration into the Turkish media field. Participants generally perceived greater freedom of expression than in their countries of origin, although this varied by subject matter, institutional affiliation, and political context. The findings suggest that Istanbul can function as a conditional media refuge, offering physical safety, professional continuity, and comparatively greater expressive space while exposing journalists to legal, economic, institutional, and political constraints.

item.title: The Effect of Broadcasting Parliamentary Proceedings on Legislative Disruption: Evidence from India
item.dc:creator: Ajit Phadnis, S. Sivanandham
item.description:
Political Communication · Ajit Phadnis, S. Sivanandham

Topics: Political communication, Media effects, Political polarization, Public opinion

Can broadcasting parliamentary proceedings encourage more responsible legislative behavior? Existing theories remain divided on whether increasing transparency through visual media enhances parliamentary functioning or, conversely, promotes grandstanding and protests. This paper examines the effects of televising the proceedings of the Indian parliament on legislative disruption – behavior that violates chamber rules. Although broadcasting was introduced to enhance transparency, multi-method evidence from 1,590 parliamentary sittings shows that the shift from print coverage to live visual broadcasting increased disruption. Original data further support the proposed mechanism: broadcasting redirected legislators’ incentives away from intra-legislative signaling and toward extra-legislative position-taking, fostering voter-oriented and sustained disruption. These findings contribute to broader debates on the effects of political communication technologies, showing that transparency reforms, while well-intentioned, can undermine institutional performance. The results suggest that decisions to broadcast parliamentary proceedings must be calibrated to the legislative context.

item.title: Narrative character networks are associated with storytelling success
item.dc:creator: Xuanjun Gong, Allison Eden, Frederic R Hopp, Anna W Wolfe, Matthew Grizzard
item.description:
Human Communication Research · Xuanjun Gong, Allison Eden, Frederic R Hopp, Anna W Wolfe, Matthew Grizzard

Topics: Narrative persuasion, Computational text analysis, Media effects, Entertainment

Abstract Narratives are central to human communication and entertainment, yet why some stories captivate audiences better than others remains poorly understood. Building on theories emphasizing character interdependence, this study introduces a network-based framework for examining storytelling success. We conceptualize narratives as networks composed of characters and their interactions and apply large-scale computational analysis to over 10,000 novels and 1,000 film screenplays. Structural features of these networks are related to storytelling success: lower clustering is associated with greater novel popularity and higher film ratings, whereas higher modularity is associated only with novel popularity and shorter path lengths only with film ratings. These findings demonstrate that storytelling success is related to how characters are structurally connected and organized. By formalizing story architecture as a measurable network, we provide a scalable framework for advancing media entertainment theory, linking cognitive models of graph learning with the structural organization of stories at scale.

item.title: Disconnected or selective? Understanding the drivers of low or no news consumption among chilean audiences
item.dc:creator: Alexis Cruz, Claudia Mellado
item.description:
Journalism · Alexis Cruz, Claudia Mellado

Topics: News avoidance, News consumption, Media use, Qualitative research

In a context of growing news disengagement, this study examines the distinction between low news consumption and news avoidance, identifies the factors shaping each approach to the news, and explores how these dynamics materialize into structured routines. The study draws on 49 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with participants from diverse regions and sociodemographic backgrounds in Chile. The findings identify two related yet distinct groups underlying low or non-existent news use: pragmatically disengaged news users, referring to participants with low levels of news consumption due to structural constraints, and active news avoiders, referring to individuals who deliberately distance themselves from news due to emotional burden, dissatisfaction, and distrust. Additionally, the study identifies two main types of routines through which individuals disengage from news: conscious and internalized avoidance routines . While the former involves deliberate efforts to regulate news exposure, the latter reflects routinized forms of disengagement that operate with little or no conscious reflection. Overall, this study advances the understanding of news disengagement by demonstrating that low news consumption and news avoidance are not interchangeable phenomena, but distinct processes shaped by different motivations and embedded in everyday practices.

item.title: Testing Hypotheses From the Social Approval Theory of Online Hate: An Analysis of 110 Million Messages From Parler
item.dc:creator: David M. Markowitz, Samuel Hardman Taylor
item.description:
Communication Research · David M. Markowitz, Samuel Hardman Taylor

Topics: Online hate speech, Social approval, Social media engagement, Toxicity

We examined how social approval motivates online hate via the social approval theory, which argues social approval signals on hate messages predict (1) more hate speech, and (2) more toxicity. Using 110 million messages from Parler (2018–2021), we observed that upvotes on hate speech posts (messages broadcast on users’ profiles to followers’ feeds) predicted a lower probability of hate speech in the next immediate post but more in the following week’s posts. Additionally, upvotes on comments (messages embedded within conversational threads) negatively predicted hate speech in the next comment but positively predicted the degree of toxicity during the next week and month. Between-person effects revealed negative immediate short-term effects but positive longer-term effects for hate speech. For comments , social disapproval (downvotes) moderated these relationships, making them less positive at weekly through quarterly time-intervals and more strongly negative at 6-months. Social approval predicts online hate in time- and message-dependent ways.

item.title: When it’s your own child: effects of media narratives on U.S. parents’ support for their LGBTQ+ teen
item.dc:creator: Marie‐Louise Mares, Yuchi Anthony Chen
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Marie‐Louise Mares, Yuchi Anthony Chen

Topics: Media effects, Parasocial interaction, Attitude change, Media narratives

Abstract Parents’ responses to their LGBTQ+ child are varied, often intense, and have important consequences for the child. To examine how media depictions may shape responses, a pre-registered online experiment of 494 parents tested effects of viewing two TV narratives, depicting either control (non-LGBTQ+) family interactions, parental rejection, gradual growth toward acceptance, or unalloyed acceptance, of a lesbian or transgender teen, on parents’ support and behavioral intentions regarding their own LGBTQ+ teen. Guided by theories of vicarious contact and inspiring media, we assessed mediation via identification with characters, and via feelings of inspiration and manipulation, testing baseline support as a moderator. Effects of condition were indirect-only, and contingent on baseline support. Among highly supportive parents, growth and acceptance narratives (vs. control) increased feelings of inspiration, which predicted positive behavioral intentions. Among less supportive parents, rejection and (unexpectedly) growth narratives reduced identification with depicted LGBTQ+ teens, indirectly decreasing support and behavioral intentions.

item.title: Promoting Support for Anti-Racism Movements and Intentions to Intervene: Effects of Common-Identity Narratives and the Moderating Role of Prior Prejudice
item.dc:creator: Yan Huang, Lan Ni, Zexin Ma, Natasha Saad
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Yan Huang, Lan Ni, Zexin Ma, Natasha Saad

Topics: Persuasion, Social identity, Narrative persuasion, Social influence

Two experiments examined whether emphasizing a common ingroup identity with racially different characters, operationalized as university affiliation with an African American character (Study 1) and parent identity with an Asian American character (Study 2), enhanced the impact of victim narratives. Findings indicate that emphasizing a common ingroup identity increased perceived similarity and identification with the character and reduced perceived social distance, which then fostered greater support toward anti-racism movements and stronger intentions to intervene. Common-identity narratives were particularly effective among participants with higher prior prejudice, and the moderation effect was mediated by reduced social distance.

item.title: How Chinese and U.S. media construct legitimacy at sea differently: A corpus-based comparative analysis of China’s distant-water fishing
item.dc:creator: Cheng Chen, Renping Liu
item.description:
Journalism · Cheng Chen, Renping Liu

Topics: Media framing, Journalism, Comparative media systems, Sentiment analysis

Journalism plays a vital role in shaping how societies interpret and legitimize global environmental controversies. This study compares how Chinese and U.S. media discursively frame China’s distant-water fishing (DWF)—a domain where environmental, economic, and geopolitical interests intersect. Using a corpus-based mixed-method approach that integrates sentiment analysis, keyword extraction, and nomination strategies, the research analyzes 167 English-language news articles from leading outlets in both countries to uncover how legitimacy is communicatively constructed within distinct media systems. The findings reveal two coherent yet contrasting framing logics. U.S. media adopt a critical and moralized framing that emphasizes illegality, environmental harm, and systemic accountability, reflecting a liberal-institutionalist orientation rooted in watchdog journalism and rule-based governance. Chinese media, in contrast, employ a more procedural and developmental framing that highlights regulation, cooperation, and economic pragmatism, reflecting a greater emphasis on institutional coordination, policy implementation, and national development priorities. The study advances comparative journalism research by linking media framing with policy paradigms, showing how institutional and communicative contexts shape the realization of ostensibly universal news values such as Negativity and Eliteness. Methodologically, it demonstrates the value of combining computational and qualitative discourse analysis to reveal patterned differences in journalistic representation. Substantively, it underscores journalism’s dual role in global environmental discourse—as both a site where legitimacy and responsibility are contested, and a communicative bridge that may either intensify conflict or foster mutual understanding in governing shared environmental commons.

item.title: Enhancing Democratic Listening in Online Discussions: The Role of Reaction Buttons, Discussion Moderation, and Large Language Models
item.dc:creator: Shota Gelovani, Philipp Müller, Hartmut Weßler, Hendrik Meyer, Louisa Pröschel, Anke Stoll, Marc Ziegele
item.description:
Political Communication · Shota Gelovani, Philipp Müller, Hartmut Weßler, Hendrik Meyer, Louisa Pröschel, Anke Stoll, Marc Ziegele

Topics: Democratic listening, Online discussion, Large Language Models, Content moderation

Political communication research in general – and research on political online discussions in particular – has previously focused on the exercise of democratic voice and thus largely neglected the complementary practice of democratic listening. Against the backdrop of a wide-spread perception that democratic listening is lacking in online discussions, we investigate whether listening can be strengthened through novel platform affordances. We developed an experimental online written discussion platform with listening-oriented reaction buttons and both human and AI moderation (based on GPT-4). We then conducted an experiment involving n = 740 respondents in 40 discussion groups (N = 4,355 comments), each lasting 30 minutes, covering three experimental conditions and a control condition. We compare the effect of (1) listening-oriented reaction buttons versus (2) a combination of these buttons and listening-oriented human discussion moderation versus (3) a combination of buttons and AI moderation on the level of democratic listening demonstrated in discussants’ textual contributions. We find that listening-oriented buttons alone do not enhance democratic listening. However, when combined with listening-oriented AI moderation, they are associated with a democratic listening rate of 27% within discussions, compared to 21% in the condition without either feature. Our findings lay the basis for the implementation of a combination of listening-oriented buttons and discussion moderation on news media websites, social media apps or dedicated discussion spaces using LLM-based chatbots.

item.title: The managed sisterhood: Gendered labor and intimacy in Chinese fashion influencer industry
item.dc:creator: Qiheng Lin, Chenyu Dong
item.description:
New Media & Society · Qiheng Lin, Chenyu Dong

Topics: Gender differences, Platform studies, Social media influencers, Digital labor

As China’s leading multi-channel network (MCN) institutions become increasingly industrialized and bureaucratic, their operations are paradoxically characterized by intensified emotional dynamics. Drawing on ethnographic research within a women-dominated fashion influencer team, this study identifies a sisterhood-based production model that embeds sisterly ties within hierarchical organizational structures. It traces the formation and collapse of this managed sisterhood. By cultivating an illusion of unity and belonging, intimacy makes labor more governable, obscuring coercion while facilitating the mobilization of emotional, aesthetic, and physical capacities. In this way, sisterhood becomes integral to production, intensifying labor and rendering precarity routine. Under platform capitalism, traditional Chinese sisterhood, once grounded in kinship and flexible resistance, is reconfigured into an occupational form of informal labor control, producing “disposable kinship” in which affective bonds become temporary and replaceable. This study challenges dominant political readings of sisterhood and demonstrates how intimacy itself becomes a mechanism of governance within platform capitalism.

item.title: The news production circuit: Tracing the implementation of constructive journalism
item.dc:creator: Jacob Christian Eriksen, Peter Bro
item.description:
Journalism · Jacob Christian Eriksen, Peter Bro

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, News production, Newsroom practices

Constructive journalism is increasingly invoked in newsroom strategies, educational programs, and professional debates. Yet scholarship has struggled to account for how constructive ambitions are implemented in practice over time. Existing research tends to cluster around partially disconnected domains – such as professional discourse, newsroom initiatives, and content and audience effects – without specifying the dynamic, on-going processes that link organizational decisions to editorial action and the resulting news products. This conceptual article addresses that gap by introducing an analytical framework – the MAP model (Mechanics, Actions, Products) – that conceptualizes implementation as recurring production pathways connecting organizational conditions, situated newswork, and published output. Implementation relies on sustaining these pathways through feedback loops that carry evaluations back into subsequent cycles of production. A pathway may be reinforced and repeated or left unsupported and abandoned, depending on whether the output’s value is registered and recognized. Together, these domains and processes constitute the news production circuit. The article demonstrates the analytical value of MAP through three distinct implementation configurations derived from recent research on constructive journalism. In doing so, it provides a vocabulary for comparative research on how journalistic practices, more generally, are implemented – and for identifying where and why implementation remains partial, uneven, or fragile.

item.title: Dependence or Interdependence? A Folk-Theories Perspective on Journalists’ and Activists’ Mutual Perceptions
item.dc:creator: Marlene Strehler-Schaaf, Charlotte Löb
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Marlene Strehler-Schaaf, Charlotte Löb

Topics: Social movements, Journalism, Journalistic roles, Public opinion

Drawing on folk theories , this study explores how mutual perceptions and experiences shape the journalist–activist relationship. We analyze data from two German interview studies: activists from diverse protest movements ( N = 33) and journalists covering them ( N = 38). Both groups tend to hold simplified views of each other’s work yet apply similar criteria when evaluating “good” journalism/activism and affirm the importance of their roles for democracy. Conflicts often arise from unmet expectations. The study offers insights into how journalism is understood in movement contexts and vice versa. It also clarifies the recently debated boundaries between journalism and activism.

item.title: How does young children’s digital resilience operate within and across homes and communities? A thematic analysis of parents and early years educators’ experiences
item.dc:creator: Simon P. Hammond, Jeanette D’Arcy, Laura Jennings-Tallent, Gray Prothero-Gibbs, Sandra El Gemayel, Harry T. Dyer
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Simon P. Hammond, Jeanette D’Arcy, Laura Jennings-Tallent, Gray Prothero-Gibbs, Sandra El Gemayel, Harry T. Dyer

Topics: Digital resilience, Social capital, Parental mediation, Qualitative methods

This paper examines how young children aged 0–5 years build digital resilience within interconnected home and community contexts. While playing, exploring, and socialising are central to early experiential learning, little is known about how parents/carers and educators support children to recognise, manage, and recover from mistakes in connected environments. Conceptualising digital resilience as a socio-ecological construct, the paper draws on findings from the TYKES project to address this gap. Using a multi-method qualitative design, the study thematically analyses semi-structured interviews with parents/carers (n = 17) and early years educators (n = 5), alongside focus groups with educators across two settings (n = 8), conducted using purposive sampling over a ten-month period (May 2024–February 2025). The paper argues that digital resilience is a relational and context-dependent process that unfolds across nested home and community environments, rather than solely within individual children or discrete settings. It highlights the importance of social capital and everyday interactions in shaping children’s emerging capacities to navigate online challenges. The paper contributes to the literature by demonstrating how parents/carers and educators actively cultivate digital resilience as an emergent capability, embedded in socio-ecological relations. The findings point to the need for more holistic and coordinated support across education systems, policymakers, industry, and governments to enable young children to thrive on the Internet.

item.title: Black technofeminism as critique of biological essentialism in AI anthropomorphization
item.dc:creator: Melissa C. Brown
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Melissa C. Brown

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Intersectionality, Generative AI, Gender representation

This article uses Black technofeminism to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) anthropomorphization coincides with racialized and gendered dehumanization. It builds on Black feminist thought to inform a qualitative audit of YouTube search media and images generated by Gemini and ChatGPT as a discourse on AI and humanity. The findings reveal how humans associated with AI are predominantly portrayed as white men, while AI entities are typically embodied as white women. In contrast, Black women are notably absent from general AI search results yet are disproportionately depicted as AI-generated entities portrayed in dehumanizing ways. Images of women generated by the multimodal large language models (MLLMs) default to whiteness. Because the models require a racial identifier in the prompt to show Black women, both MLLMs distort their features, including favoring lighter skin and looser hair textures as ‘more feminine.’ I argue that AI visual culture reinforces hierarchical power relations by embedding biologically deterministic constructs of humanity, rooted in racial and gender essentialism, into digital environments. It therefore concludes that Black technofeminism resituates understandings of intersectionality in the study of racial and gender bias as a critique of power, revealing AI's paradoxical implementation as a tool of progress and an instrument of oppression.

item.title: War, Feelings of Belonging, and News Diets: How Russia’s Full-Scale Invasion of Ukraine Did (Not) Change the News Repertoires of Russian Speakers in Germany
item.dc:creator: Anna Ryzhova, Eunike Piwoni, Florian Toepfl
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Anna Ryzhova, Eunike Piwoni, Florian Toepfl

Topics: News consumption, Media use, Social media, Disinformation

This study examines how Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched in February 2022, has influenced the news repertoires of first-generation Russian-speaking migrants living in Germany. While previous research suggests that news consumption patterns are typically stable, it has also shown that major disruptive events - such as the COVID-19 pandemic - have the potential for significant shifts. However, little research has explored how wars impact the transnational news repertoires of migrant communities. Grounded in 25 semi-structured interviews, the study demonstrates that the four types of news repertoires identified by previous research on Russian speakers in Germany prior to 2022 remained valid. Although very few participants indicated that they had completely switched repertoire type, nuanced changes were observed within the four types. These changes were accompanied by a complex process of renegotiating their sense of belonging to Russia. Moreover, across the four types, there was a spike in news use in the first weeks of the full-scale war, followed by news avoidance, and a “migration” to the platform Telegram. This study advances research on diasporic news repertoires, digital war, and disinformation by showing that geopolitical crises can shape the news repertoires of transnational audiences who have feelings of belonging to actors involved in conflict.

item.title: Negotiating Infrastructural Integration: Cloud Services and the Evolution of News Website Ecosystems in France and the Netherlands
item.dc:creator: Agustin Ferrari Braun, Fernando van der Vlist, Thomas Poell
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Agustin Ferrari Braun, Fernando van der Vlist, Thomas Poell

Topics: Digital platforms, Journalism, Digital journalism, Digital media

This paper analyzes the infrastructural integration of European news media with digital platforms and third-party service providers between 2015–2025. Reviewing current research, we note increased scholarly attention to the infrastructural relations between news organizations and digital platforms. Yet, despite this heightened interest, we are still missing a systematic empirical examination of how infrastructural integration shapes the spaces of negotiation between news media and tech companies. We provide such an examination through a historical analysis of the top ten news websites in France and the Netherlands, using a custom version of the 4CAT Capture and Analysis Toolkit on 9,456 archived snapshots. The analysis of evolving third-party service (de-)integrations, highlight the rise of audiovisual content and the decline of website analytics, as well as broader industry and regulatory developments (e.g., GDPR). These changes in website architectures point to shifting strategies of news organizations to adapt and preserve their independence in an online environment increasingly dominated by digital platforms. Yet, paradoxically, those strategies are enabled by cloud infrastructures provided by the same platform companies, deepening the dependence of news organizations on these companies. Thus, infrastructural integration is a process of demarcation of spaces and activities between news organizations and tech companies.

item.title: Monitoring Electoral Democracy: Discovering and Reusing Text and Multimedia Data for Political Communication Research
item.dc:creator: Jakob‐Moritz Eberl, Jana Bernhard-Harrer, Mariken Anna Catharina Geertruida van der Velden, Sofía Gil‐Clavel, Paul Balluff, Johannes B. Gruber, Noëlle S. Lebernegg, Kasper Welbers, Marvin Stecker, Claes H. de Vreese
item.description:
Media and Communication · Jakob‐Moritz Eberl, Jana Bernhard-Harrer, Mariken Anna Catharina Geertruida van der Velden, Sofía Gil‐Clavel, Paul Balluff, Johannes B. Gruber, Noëlle S. Lebernegg, Kasper Welbers, Marvin Stecker, Claes H. de Vreese

Topics: Political communication, Communication research, Digital media, Content analysis

Political communication research relies on a fragmented landscape of media sources, text and multimedia corpora, analytical tools, and research workflows. Researchers face two related barriers: identifying which resources exist and determining whether and under what conditions they can be accessed and reused. This article presents Monitoring Electoral Democracy (MEDem), a distributed European research infrastructure for comparative political communication research, with particular attention to its Service Center for Text and Multimedia Data. The Service Center develops two complementary services: MEDem Meteor provides a curated, knowledge-graph-based discovery layer that connects media sources, datasets, archives, analytical tools, and publications; MEDem Amsterdam Content Analysis Toolkit supports the hosting, controlled reuse, and non-consumptive analysis of text and multimedia corpora. Together, the services address discovery and access as interconnected infrastructural problems. MEDem Meteor makes dispersed resources, relationships, and coverage gaps visible, while MEDem Amsterdam Content Analysis Toolkit makes access conditions transparent and enables reuse without redistributing protected content. This combination can reduce duplicated data collection, support more theoretically informed source selection, and strengthen cumulative and comparative research. Its realization, however, depends on sustained curation, community participation, and long-term institutional commitment.

item.title: Can AI Gauge Deliberative Quality? Evaluating Deliberation on Social Media With Large Language Models
item.dc:creator: Patrick Frey, Smita Bhattacharya, Gregor Wiedemann, Cornelius Puschmann
item.description:
Media and Communication · Patrick Frey, Smita Bhattacharya, Gregor Wiedemann, Cornelius Puschmann

Topics: Large Language Models, Political polarization, Civic engagement, Social media

Although social media has become a central arena for deliberative discourse, debates are frequently characterized by incivility. Due to the volume of online discourse, it is challenging to assess when and where interventions, such as community-based counterspeech, are required. Accordingly, automated measurement of deliberative quality is a powerful tool for facilitating constructive online communication. Since deliberation is multidimensional, attempts to monitor online discourse must consider alternative forms of communication to foster inclusive deliberation. Whereas Type I deliberative dimensions, such as rationality and civility, are grounded in Habermasian ideals, Type II deliberation extends this perspective by incorporating alternative communicative forms, including emotionality and storytelling, into a more inclusive assessment of deliberative quality. Addressing the limitations of prior studies that primarily focused on classic Type I deliberative dimensions and tested only a small number of large language models, this study evaluates multiple open-weight models to conduct a nuanced assessment of deliberative quality. We applied the large language model that achieved the best overall balance between predictive performance, model size, and computational efficiency to a dataset of 64,223 comments from German-language climate change discourse on X. Our results demonstrate that large language models can reliably capture complex Type II deliberative dimensions despite class imbalances and subtle linguistic cues that generally hinder automated text classification. Class imbalance often impairs classification performance due to highly skewed label distributions, and Type II dimensions are particularly difficult to detect as they are often signaled by implicit, context-dependent markers. The empirical analysis also reveals distinct communicative patterns: While public speakers predominantly employ civil, rational, constructive, and common-good-oriented communication, other debating users exhibit higher levels of reciprocal engagement, humor, and negative emotions, alongside more frequent incivility. Our study demonstrates that AI-driven measurement can serve as a foundational tool for identifying norm violations, directing counterspeech toward specific debates, promoting inclusive digital public spheres, and observing broader long-term effects of moderation and interventions on the quality of debate.

item.title: Positioning enjoyment and appreciation as key components of news use
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Hoewe, Brett Sherrick, Diane L. Jackson, Sam Woodland
item.description:
Journal of Communication · Jennifer Hoewe, Brett Sherrick, Diane L. Jackson, Sam Woodland

Topics: News consumption, Media use, Affective polarization, Entertainment media

Abstract In response to the continued convergence and hybridization of news and entertainment media content, this research explores the roles of enjoyment and appreciation in contemporary news use. Three studies (two surveys and one experiment) show a clear link between enjoyment, appreciation, and news use. Both enjoyment and appreciation are positively related to agreement, value alignment, attitude change, and attitude reinforcement in the context of news use. News enjoyment is related to increased positive and decreased negative emotions, while news appreciation is connected to an increase in and tolerance of mixed emotions. Importantly, news enjoyment decreases actual knowledge while facilitating greater affective polarization. News appreciation increases more positive feelings toward other people. These results illustrate the value of merging research on entertainment and news media, and they also suggest that news enjoyment is a driving factor in the growth of less democratic news use outcomes.

item.title: Content escalation, content homogenization, and user immersion: a three-dimensional conceptualization of online rabbit holes
item.dc:creator: Ine Beyens, Qiru Huo, Konrad Mikalauskas, Rebecca Godard, Amber van der Wal
item.description:
Annals of the ICA · Ine Beyens, Qiru Huo, Konrad Mikalauskas, Rebecca Godard, Amber van der Wal

Topics: Algorithmic curation, Echo chambers, Content moderation, Social media algorithms

Abstract Online environments are often described as drawing users into a “rabbit hole.” While the term is frequently invoked in both academic and popular discourse, there is little consensus on what precisely constitutes an online rabbit hole. This lack of consensus has resulted in research on this phenomenon being conceptually fragmented and inconsistent. The current scoping review addresses this gap by systematically examining how online rabbit holes have been conceptualized and operationalized. Through a critical synthesis of 30 studies, we derive three recurring dimensions in the different conceptualizations of the online rabbit hole: content escalation, content homogenization, and user immersion. Building on these three key dimensions, we propose a comprehensive three-dimensional conceptual framework for understanding online rabbit holes and offer recommendations for accurately measuring and detecting them.

item.title: The democratic value of local information: How journalistic and non-journalistic sources relate to community attachment, civic engagement, and democratic attitudes
item.dc:creator: Leyla Dogruel, Jakob Henke, Wiebke Moehring
item.description:
Journalism · Leyla Dogruel, Jakob Henke, Wiebke Moehring

Topics: Local news, Civic engagement, Media use, Political participation

This study investigates the relationship between local information use, community integration, and political attitudes within the German context. Drawing on representative survey data from 2069 citizens, we examine how using journalistic and non-journalistic local information sources, specifically official municipal sources, community-based sources and interpersonal communication, relates to community attachment, civic engagement, satisfaction with local democracy, and trust in local politics. Results indicate that, consistent with previous scholarship, frequent local media use is positively associated with stronger community attachment, higher civic engagement, and more favorable evaluations of local politics and local democracy. Compared to non-journalistic sources of information, local media emerged as stronger predictors of community attachment, satisfaction with local democracy, and trust in local politics, but not civic engagement. Our findings highlight the need for closer examination of how the growing diversity of local information sources impact community integration and civic engagements in an increasingly hybrid media environment.

item.title: Invisible Women in Economics: Almost Two Centuries of Gender Representation in the Financial Times and The Economist (1843–2021)
item.dc:creator: Andrea Barigazzi
item.description:
Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly · Andrea Barigazzi

Topics: Gender representation, Journalism studies, Content analysis, News coverage

This study examines gender representation in the Financial Times and The Economist between 1843 and 2021. Using millions of articles and name-frequency analysis, it traces the long-term evolution of women’s visibility in economic news. Results reveal a U -shaped pattern: relatively high representation in the nineteenth century, a decline through much of the 20th century, and a gradual recovery since the 1980s. Comparisons with benchmarks of women’s participation in high-status occupations and economic sectors show a persistent gap between media visibility and real-world presence. The findings point to a lasting paper ceiling in economic journalism. JEL codes: J16, N34, L82

item.title: Digital transformation in Public Service Media: Adaptation strategies of European broadcasters
item.dc:creator: Clara Almeida Santos, Felisbela Lopes
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Clara Almeida Santos, Felisbela Lopes

Topics: Digital transformation, Public service media, Platformization, Digital platforms
