Guided by uncertainty reduction theory (URT), this study examined how headset use and familiarity jointly influence social presence, closeness, ostracism, and group interaction dynamics in face-to-face MR group collaboration. University students (N = 101) were assigned to groups of 9–10 participants to either wear a headset or not before engaging in a discussion task. Compared to participants with headsets, participants without headsets felt less close to and less present with headset-wearing partners. In contrast, headset wearers, who could see the other group members via passthrough video, did not exhibit parallel decreases. Behavioral analyses showed a crossover pattern in compromise behavior, where individuals who wore a headset compromised more in unfamiliar settings (i.e. where they rated group members less familiar) but those who did not wear a headset compromised more in familiar settings, suggesting that individuals adapt communication strategies to manage uncertainty in asymmetric MR environments. Overall, MR headsets selectively affected interpersonal connection and group dynamics.

item.title: Heterogeneities of Smartphone Use Among Chinese Urban Older Adults: A Life Course Approach
item.dc:creator: Lu Chen, Miaoting Cheng
item.description:
Mobile Media & Communication · Lu Chen, Miaoting Cheng

Topics: Smartphone use, Older adults, Life course, Digital inequality

Drawing on a qualitative analysis of semi-structured interview data, this research adopts a life course perspective to examine how Chinese urban older adults adjust their smartphone use in response to significant life events across later life. The findings reveal that multi-level life events foster a dynamic continuum of (dis)connection. At the same time, adaptive and maladaptive use patterns coexist among Chinese urban older adults, demonstrating heterogeneity in their smartphone use. By proposing a shift from an age-as-variable approach to an aging-as-process approach, this study emphasizes older adults’ contextualized (dis)connectivity situated within life course transitions and trajectories, which reflects a negotiation between individual agency and socio-technical structures.

item.title: Data benefits? Attitudes and aspirations of recipients towards social security administrative data sharing
item.dc:creator: Victoria Gorton, Morgan E. Currie
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Victoria Gorton, Morgan E. Currie

Topics: Public attitudes, Trust, Digital inequality, Data sharing

This paper outlines benefit recipients’ views towards the sharing of data that is collected about them when they routinely interact with social security services. Sharing this administrative data between public bodies promises to transform the delivery and evaluation of social security. However, there remains a lack of research into public attitudes, understandings, and aspirations for the sharing of this data, particularly from those whose data would be shared. Drawing on discussions from deliberative focus groups with 41 individuals, we reflect on the scope for increased data sharing to deliver improvements for recipients.While participants were aware of how their data is currently shared and how increased data sharing might have advantages, they expressed strong distrust in government agencies to manage their data and concerns about being placed in a position of increased vulnerability. We argue individuals’ views towards data sharing cannot be separated from their lived experiences of data systems – their data realities – which are often markedly different from system designers. We conclude by offering considerations against data systems re-introducing paternalistic policy, unintentionally, via automation – which we term ‘automated paternalism’.

item.title: From mobilization to diversion: a comparative study of wartime communication tactics of Ukrainian and Russian political elites on Telegram
item.dc:creator: Mykola Makhortykh, Aytalina Kulichkina, Kateryna Maikovska
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Mykola Makhortykh, Aytalina Kulichkina, Kateryna Maikovska

Topics: Political communication, Telegram, Crisis communication, Political polarization

This study examines how Ukrainian and Russian political elites communicate on Telegram during the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war. Using a dataset of Telegram public posts from 2019 to 2024, we analyze changes in communication volume, thematic content, and actor engagement before and after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion. While the invasion triggered a massive spike in elites’ activity on Telegram in both countries—most notably among actors associated with Russia’s ruling pro-regime party—the focus of this communication diverged sharply. While Ukrainian elites initially prioritized war-related mobilization, this emphasis has declined over time. By contrast, Russian elites from the start adopted a tactic of strategic diversion, avoiding discussion of the war and shifting public attention to unrelated issues, such as crises in the West. Finally, we show that communication patterns are stratified by party size, with smaller parties specializing in narrow policy niches. These findings shed light on how political elites adapt their communication strategies in online environments during wartime.

item.title: Trust in algorithms biased appraisal and boosted affect in online dating
item.dc:creator: Jian Ming Hu, Yoo Jung Oh
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Jian Ming Hu, Yoo Jung Oh

Topics: Online dating, Trust, Algorithmic curation, Social media algorithms

The algorithmification of social encounters is a topic of immense scholarly interest. People often form layperson beliefs about how algorithms work, which can predict how people psychologically navigate algorithmic social encounters. Online dating scholars have drawn upon correlational findings to speculate that trust in algorithms primes daters to think and feel about their dating experiences in certain ways. Within a sample of U.S. adults (N = 165), we experimentally test this speculation by manipulating participants’ trusting beliefs in the efficacy of algorithms (high vs. low), assigning them to evaluate online dating profiles drawn from the same pool, and observing whether appraisal and emotion differed between conditions. Post profile evaluation, high-belief participants perceived higher online dating success than low-belief participants. In turn, more successful participants felt more self-assured and jovial, and meanwhile less anxious or sad. Our study is the first to experimentally examine trusting beliefs in dating algorithms. Findings suggest a self-fulfilling prophecy of beliefs about algorithmic social processes and warrant more future investigation.

item.title: Between Journalism and Justice: Disciplinary Humility in Open-Source Investigations
item.dc:creator: Isabella Regan, Imar de Vries
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Isabella Regan, Imar de Vries

Topics: Journalism, Open-source investigations, Professional norms, Digital journalism

Open-source investigations (OSI) have become an increasingly influential method for reporting on conflict, documenting human rights violations, and supporting justice and accountability efforts. As the field has matured, OSI practitioners have increasingly operated across journalistic, legal, human rights, and technical domains, creating innovation and collaboration opportunities, but also disciplinary tensions. Despite growing scholarship on the institutionalization of OSI, less attention has been paid to how practitioners navigate overlapping disciplinary mandates. Drawing on interviews with 35 practitioners involved in OSI across journalism, human rights, law enforcement and specialized investigative organizations, this article examines how disciplinary boundaries are experienced and responded to within justice and accountability contexts. The findings show that practitioners respond to tensions between journalistic and legal norms through forms of boundary recalibration, including recognizing disciplinary limitations and restructuring investigative work. To explain these dynamics, this article introduces disciplinary humility, defined as the recognition of the limits of one’s disciplinary expertise and mandate when operating across overlapping professional jurisdictions. The article contributes to digital journalism scholarship by showing that the OSI institutionalization is shaped not only by hybridity and boundary crossing, but also by boundary recalibration through which practitioners re-examine expertise and mandates across journalistic and legal contexts.

item.title: Between Ideals and BoPo: Daily Associations Between Exposure to Appearance Content and Body Image Among Young Individuals with Visible Differences
item.dc:creator: Laure Dedecker, L. Coosemans, Chelly Maes, Lara Schreurs, Laura Vandenbosch
item.description:
Media Psychology · Laure Dedecker, L. Coosemans, Chelly Maes, Lara Schreurs, Laura Vandenbosch

Topics: Body image, Social media use, Social media algorithms, Mental health

Exposure to appearance-related content, including beauty ideals and body positivity (BoPo) elements, is linked to young individuals’ body image. Despite being challenged to develop a healthy body image, research has overlooked young individuals with visible differences. This daily diary study among a community-recruited sample of 117 Dutch-speaking (i.e. 110 Belgians, 7 Dutch) young individuals with visible differences (Mage = 25.41), therefore, examined the short-term relationships between exposure to beauty ideals and BoPo elements with/without visible differences and appearance satisfaction, and body/visible difference surveillance. Also, the moderating role of protective filtering was explored. Multilevel regression models showed that on days when participants saw more beauty ideals without visible differences, they showed less appearance satisfaction, and higher body/visible difference surveillance, compared to their typical daily exposure and body image levels. Protective filtering moderated this association: individuals high in protective filtering experienced smaller decreases in appearance satisfaction. No between- or other within-person associations emerged. These findings highlight the complexity of social media exposure for the body image of young individuals with visible differences and the value of enhancing their protective filtering.

item.title: Platformed affective withdrawal: Quiet quitting and the refusal of gendered emotional labour on TikTok
item.dc:creator: Aybüke KAPLAN
item.description:
New Media & Society · Aybüke KAPLAN

Topics: Short-form video, TikTok, Digital labor, Platform studies

This article examines #quietquitting on TikTok as a platform-mediated articulation of gendered affective withdrawal. While organisational research interprets quiet quitting as reduced discretionary effort or declining work engagement, this study examines how quiet quitting is articulated as a digitally circulated refusal of feminised emotional labour. Drawing on feminist theories of affective labour and critical platform studies, the analysis explores how workers renegotiate expectations of emotional availability within algorithmically structured visibility regimes. The study is based on a qualitative-dominant mixed-methods analysis of 586 TikTok videos shared under #quietquitting between 2020 and 2026. Combining thematic discourse analysis with descriptive engagement indicators, the findings show that creators frequently frame quiet quitting as a refusal of unpaid relational mediation, emotional management, and workplace care. The article introduces the concept of platformed affective withdrawal to explain how narratives of workplace disengagement circulate through algorithmic visibility systems that amplify and individualise gendered labour inequalities.

item.title: Praise, rent, and the platform: Substack and the enclosure of blog culture
item.dc:creator: Will Riley
item.description:
New Media & Society · Will Riley

Topics: Platform studies, Platformization, Digital labour, Social media platforms

This article situates Substack within the platformisation of blogging and the enclosure of cultural production within proprietary infrastructures. Tracing the genealogy of blogging as a decentralised practice that carried within it the seeds of citizen journalism and informal intellectual life, I argue that Substack does not restore an apparently lost cultural practice but renegotiates and interpolates blogging into a platformised logic. Framed as a return to independent, writer-led publishing, Substack instead, as I argue, renders free-labour interaction as a source of rent. I analyse the rhetoric and revolving discourse around Substack’s internal curatorial project, ‘The Substack Post’. Drawing on Jodi Dean’s account of blogs as displaced mediators alongside theories of digital labour and platform capitalism, and approaching Substack as a simultaneously platformised and infrastructuralised formation, I argue that praise operates as a platform-specific form of commodity fetishism, animating the platform while obscuring the labour relations that sustain it.

item.title: Reconfiguring repression: Violence against journalists in Indonesia under democratic backsliding (2014–2025)
item.dc:creator: Wisnu Prasetya Utomo
item.description:
Journalism · Wisnu Prasetya Utomo

Topics: Press freedom, Journalism, Political communication, Digital harassment

Violence against journalists in Indonesia has been reconfigured as a broader system of repression under democratic backsliding. This article examines how repression adapts under such conditions by conceptualizing violence as authoritarian innovation. Repression is redistributed across forms, perpetrators, and targets, preserving deniability while maintaining disciplinary effects. Analyzing 780 documented incidents (2014–2025) from the Alliance of Independent Journalists (AJI), the study codes violence across forms (physical, digital, legal, obstruction), perpetrators (state actors, non-state actors, unknown), and targets (individual journalists, media organizations). The analysis traces violence’s longitudinal reconfiguration under democratic backsliding. Three patterns emerge. First, physical attacks persist but increasingly coexist with digital harassment and obstruction. Second, perpetrator attribution becomes increasingly opaque, with unknown actors responsible for more incidents than police or non-state actors by 2025. Third, attacks targeting media organizations rise sixfold. The findings extend authoritarian innovation and press freedom scholarship, revealing how repression adapts temporally through accumulation and layering.

item.title: Quietly taking sides: The machine habitus and metaphorical framing in human and LLM-generated news
item.dc:creator: Xiaoshuang Guo
item.description:
Journalism · Xiaoshuang Guo

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Generative AI, Large Language Models, Journalistic practice

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to draft the news. These systems may frame the news differently from human journalists. In particular, it remains less understood how they handle metaphor, a potent framing tool in news discourse. Following Bourdieu’s field theory, we compare LLMs’ metaphorical framing with the journalistic habitus of human reporting in two studies of German news on Chinese investment spanning a quarter century (with 2975 metaphors from human journalism and 1924 from LLM-generated news writing), and conduct a prompting experiment across four instructions and three recent LLMs (DeepSeek V4, GPT-5.5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5) with 4877 metaphors. We find that compared to journalists that favored deliberate, evaluatively charged figurative expressions, the LLM-generated news was conventional by default, framing investment as a procedural, depoliticized process. We regard this disposition as a “machine habitus”. It proved durable across prompted years and model versions, bound to a closed set of source domains, and generative , varying under instruction only within that set. Its conceptual sources and deliberateness moved sharply with the prompt, yet showed little variation across LLMs, while its evaluative orientation tracked the prompt, with only weak differences by model origin. Across two versions of LLMs, the disposition proved more durable than the volume of metaphor it governs: the newer LLMs wrote more figuratively yet remained conflict-averse. The study contributes to debates on automation, framing, and accountability in journalism.

item.title: A genealogy of conceptual confusion: Epistemological fault lines across media-ritual concepts
item.dc:creator: Hung-Yen Hsu
item.description:
European Journal of Communication · Hung-Yen Hsu

Topics: Communication theory, Media effects, Mediatization, Communication science

Research on media–ritual intersections deploys seven concepts: media events, media rituals, mediatized rituals, media ritualization, ritual mediatization, ritual media, and ritualized media. Their overlap generates unmarked substitution between analytically divergent registers. The slippage is a structural consequence of three epistemological tributaries (Durkheimian social theory, Carey's ritual view, and mediatization theory), each foregrounding a different dimension of the same phenomena. Genealogical analysis diagnoses four confusions: process conflated with product, unmarked shifting among power paradigms, materiality–practice divergence, and directional inversion. Three fault lines (integration vs. domination, process vs. structure, exceptional vs. everyday) constitute a meta-theoretical framework. The article advances positioned conceptual deployment: researchers specify their coordinates along all three dimensions. The seven concepts serve as a diagnostic case: concept use in communication research presupposes epistemological commitments, marked or not. An under-theorized intersection, mediatized ritualization, is advanced as a provisional theoretical proposition about how platform architectures may reshape ritualized media practice.

item.title: The Politics of the “Non-Political”: A Conceptual Review
item.dc:creator: Yufan Guo, Yibin Fan
item.description:
Political Communication · Yufan Guo, Yibin Fan

Topics: Political communication, Communication theory, Political polarization, Depoliticization

Recent literature has documented a growing entanglement between political processes and many nonpolitical entities. This calls into question the traditional presupposition of politics as a self-contained sphere, highlighting the need to clarify how the conceptual relationship between the political and the nonpolitical has been established. In line with a relational understanding of politics, we provide a boundary analysis by looking at the “non-political” labeling in 140 empirical studies published in political science and communication journals. Two major conceptual treatments are identified: categorical, treating the “non-political” as an inherent, exclusive feature; and contextual, viewing it as a temporary, transformative state. Intellectual traditions, theoretical orientations, methodological standards, and rhetorical norms in academic knowledge production may explain why this boundary has been constructed in such different ways. We call for a more active reconciliation between these treatments, and argue that the nonpolitical, as well as (de)politicization, should be recognized as a meaningful analytical lens. It signifies a relational stance against the explicit, institutionalized politics in political communication studies, offering an indirect yet heuristically productive response to the question of what the political is.

item.title: “Hogwarts is My Home.” The Influence of Transportation, Identification, and Emotion-Specific Personality Traits on the Perceived Sense of Heimat in Fictional Media Worlds
item.dc:creator: Holger Schramm, Julia Grunwald
item.description:
Journal of Broadcasting & Electronic Media · Holger Schramm, Julia Grunwald

Topics: Parasocial relationships, Media psychology, Uses and gratifications, Well-being

In the course of globalization, people are often uprooted from their geographical homes and satisfy their need for a sense of home (sense of Heimat) through alternative sources. Until now, fictional media worlds have hardly been studied in this context, even though fiction has been shown to satisfy social needs. The results of a stimulus-based online survey, in which participants watched an excerpt from the film “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone,” show that transportation into the fictional world and identification with Harry Potter can promote a sense of Heimat and, as a result, positive affect.

item.title: Methods Hub: A Community-Driven, Interactive Platform for Open-Source Computational Tools and Tutorials
item.dc:creator: Christina Viehmann, Johannes Kiesel, Arnim Bleier, Chung-hong Chan, Po-Chun Chang, Raniere Silva, Ahrabhi Kathirgamalingam, Taimoor Khan, Stephan Linzbach, Fakhri Momeni
item.description:
Media and Communication · Christina Viehmann, Johannes Kiesel, Arnim Bleier, Chung-hong Chan, Po-Chun Chang, Raniere Silva, Ahrabhi Kathirgamalingam, Taimoor Khan, Stephan Linzbach, Fakhri Momeni

Topics: Computational methods, Open science, Research methodology, Digital methods

As computational methods become increasingly central to social science research, there is a growing demand for research software infrastructures that are sustainable, grounded in principles of open science, and embedded in the community. In response, we are introducing the Methods Hub as an open-source, community-driven collection of computational tools designed to support social science research in solving complex data-related tasks. The Methods Hub integrates three complementary components: First, quality-curated content, including computational methods and accompanying tutorials, which are specifically presented from a social science research perspective. Second, the methods and tutorials are hosted on a web portal enabling researchers to discover, apply, learn, and publish computational methods. Third, interactive, browser-based execution backends allow users to directly run, test, and adapt the code of methods and tutorials. These components are guided by a set of core principles: a long-term infrastructure perspective, reproducibility requirements, and a focus on community. The Methods Hub builds a long-term infrastructure that extends beyond the scope of single projects. Further, reproducibility functions as a quality assurance measure while advancing the practices of open science. Finally, the Methods Hub is built on public, community-based submissions by treating research software as citable academic output and providing visibility, accessibility, and formal recognition. We are also broadening the community by fostering learning and ease of access. Looking ahead, the Methods Hub is exploring the potential of AI as both a research tool and to further strengthen the infrastructure, while maintaining transparency, reproducibility, and quality standards for computational social science research.

item.title: A Framework for Classifying Uncertainties in AI-Driven Newsrooms
item.dc:creator: Luna Paladino, Paula Castro Pires de Souza Chimenti, André Fonseca
item.description:
Media and Communication · Luna Paladino, Paula Castro Pires de Souza Chimenti, André Fonseca

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Generative AI, Newsroom practices, Journalistic practice

This study examines how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is adopted and integrated into the newsroom of a major Brazilian media organization—Globo. While AI deployment in journalism has expanded globally, the experiences lived by journalists in contexts that are not Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic remain underexplored. Combining in-depth interviews, internal documents, organizational presentations, public materials, and direct observation within a qualitative case study, this study analyzes how GAI is reshaping newsroom practices, routines, and professional identities. It introduces a framework for classifying uncertainties in AI-driven newsrooms, a type II theory, which is designed to describe, classify, and organize the main forms of uncertainty faced by journalists when interacting with GAI systems, and then structure these uncertainties into three analytical levels—macro (ecosystem), meso (organization), and micro (identity)—while pairing each level with its associated coping strategies. Given its single-case basis, the framework is presented as a possible framework whose analytical categories require further empirical application before broader validation.

item.title: Proxies in Print: Strategic Narratives of the Sudan Conflict in Digital Media
item.dc:creator: Téwodros W. Workneh
item.description:
Media and Communication · Téwodros W. Workneh

Topics: Media framing, News coverage, Political communication, Digital media

The Sudanese civil war exemplifies how contemporary proxy conflicts are fiercely contested within digital information ecologies. Utilizing strategic narrative theory, this study examines the structural weaponization of transnational journalism to construct the geopolitical ontology of state collapse. An interpretive analysis of 402 English-language articles from Qatar’s Al Jazeera English, the UAE’s The National, and the US’s The New York Times reveals significant divergences in narrative projection. The New York Times frames the crisis through a “global instability” index, actively legitimizing US-led diplomatic intervention. Al Jazeera English deploys an identity narrative of “state victimhood” to delegitimize rival paramilitaries and subtextually indict competing Gulf patrons. In stark contrast, The National exercises “humanitarian obfuscation,” actively depoliticizing the disaster to shield Emirati proxy interventions from international scrutiny. These findings demonstrate that democratic and authoritarian regimes alike systematically co-opt digital news platforms as soft power arsenals to dictate the geopolitical imaginaries of the Global South.

item.title: Social Media “Image Operations” During the Tigray War (2020–2022)
item.dc:creator: Matti Pohjonen, Amanuel Tesfaye Kebede
item.description:
Media and Communication · Matti Pohjonen, Amanuel Tesfaye Kebede

Topics: Social media, Visual communication, Social media analysis, Political communication

This article examines the use of social media images during the Tigray War (2020–2022), one of the world’s deadliest armed conflicts of the 21st century. Drawing on a corpus of 92.9 million tweets and over 500,000 images shared on Twitter, we analyse what types of images were shared by the opposing sides of the conflict and what specific functions these images served in antagonistic information campaigns. The article shows how images were used not only to amplify the opposing strategic narratives about war but also to shape the emotional or affective registers related to it. The pro-Tigray campaign relied on the heavy use of emotive images of casualties as well as images of material destruction, which, combined with the use of infographics, collectively conveyed victimhood with the goal of putting pressure on the Ethiopian government and its allies. The pro-government side, in turn, relied more on images that tried to evoke patriotism and resistance in the audience, organise protests, as well as represent a stance of anti-colonial defiance against international pressure. The article contributes to the growing literature on digital media in contemporary conflicts by proposing a novel research framework and methodology and providing original empirical findings on an understudied dimension of contemporary conflicts.

item.title: The Metajournalistic Discourse and the Sociopolitical Construction of AI Risk in Chinese Journalism
item.dc:creator: J. Zhang
item.description:
Media and Communication · J. Zhang

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Journalistic practice, Journalistic roles, Media systems

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into journalism has improved production efficiency but raised concerns about its potential to compromise content quality and undermine journalists’ professional capacity. These tensions are particularly pronounced in China, where AI deployment in journalism intersects with state-led advocacy and professional authority. Drawing on metajournalistic discourse and taking a sociopolitical perspective, I examine how journalistic discourse frames and responds to AI risks in structurally constrained contexts. I conducted a textual analysis of 102 articles published between 2022 and 2025 by Chinese journalists affiliated with institutional media. These articles narrate journalists’ perceptions of, or working experiences with, AI. AI risks are discursively framed at three levels: content quality, mainstream values, and professional subjectivity. Journalistic discourse constructs an asymmetrical attribution of these risks, assigning responsibility primarily to opaque AI systems, technology companies, and individual journalists positioned as “risk filters,” while largely overlooking the responsibilities of media organizations and the state. Political intervention, institutional hierarchy, and professional commitments shape adaptive boundary work that aligns with state-led AI advocacy while establishing boundaries by limiting AI capability in journalistic work. This study provides an empirical account of how journalists negotiate AI risks and professional autonomy amid advanced AI development and state-sanctioned boundaries, extending Western-centric and Global South research.

item.title: Finding Love in the Black Box: Algorithm Awareness on Dating Apps
item.dc:creator: Doris Bukman, Liesel L. Sharabi, Elisabeth Timmermans
item.description:
Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking · Doris Bukman, Liesel L. Sharabi, Elisabeth Timmermans

Topics: Online dating, Algorithm awareness, Trust, Human-computer interaction

Most dating apps use algorithms to match users to one another, but are not fully transparent about how their recommender systems work. In turn, users have varying degrees of awareness of matching algorithms. Unfortunately, little is known about how awareness of algorithmic functioning relates to online dating. This research examined the relationship between algorithm awareness, trust in algorithms, and satisfaction with the quality of matches. A survey was conducted among 500 users of the Dutch dating app Breeze, presented to respondents within the app itself. Relationships were estimated with structural equation modeling. Higher algorithm awareness was associated with more trust in algorithms, which positively related to satisfaction with the quality of matches. This mediated association between awareness and satisfaction with matches suggested that awareness of matching algorithms is associated with better outcomes of dating app use. This research contributes to the limited literature on human-algorithm interaction on dating apps. Overall, the results suggest that algorithm awareness may be a relevant part of the online dating experience.

item.title: Not only correcting lies. Analysis of interventionist strategies in news articles dealing with misinformation during the COVID-19 pandemic in the Netherlands
item.dc:creator: David Blanco‐Herrero, Toni G.L.A. van der Meer, Bas van den Putte
item.description:
Journalism · David Blanco‐Herrero, Toni G.L.A. van der Meer, Bas van den Putte

Topics: Misinformation, Journalistic roles, Health communication, COVID-19 pandemic

During crises, when falsehoods often spread faster than facts, journalists face the challenge of deciding how to fight misinformation without amplifying its reach. This study focuses on Dutch journalists who addressed pandemic-related misinformation during the COVID-19 crisis (January 2020–May 2023), distinguishing between actively interventionist strategies (correction and prebunking) and more detached approaches. Drawing on a content analysis of 698 news articles, it investigates the use of actively interventionist strategies, and their variation across pandemic phases and in their use of expert sources. Findings show that 14.2% of articles adopted actively interventionist roles, with corrections being more common than prebunking. Such strategies were more frequent during the initial uncertain phase of the pandemic and during vaccine rollouts. Articles using these strategies relied on a greater number and diversity of sources, especially academic, governmental, and health-related. The results highlight a cautious engagement by journalists in actively countering misinformation, favoring a more detached reporting. Overall, the study advances the understanding of journalistic role performance in health crises and the interplay between journalism practice and misinformation management.

item.title: Young people and the data gaze: experiencing datafication in everyday life
item.dc:creator: Julia E. Coffey, Steven Threadgold
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Julia E. Coffey, Steven Threadgold

Topics: Datafication, Digital media, Young people, Digital platforms

Young people’s capacity to see and know themselves is increasingly informed by algorithmic and classificatory logics. In this article, we extend Beer’s concept of the data gaze, drawing from qualitative empirical examples to illustrate how young people navigate and incorporate datafied ways of seeing and knowing in their everyday practices via engagement with financial technology (fintech) and photo editing apps. We argue that whilst young people are increasingly ‘gazed upon’ in their interactions with fintech and image-editing apps, that is, categorised and imagined by algorithmic and machinic processes, they also gaze back. We explore two specific aspects of the broader data gaze: (1) datafied money and the financialised gaze that young people experience when being nudged while using gamified fintech services, and (2) datafied bodies and the forensic gaze young people use to inform selfie-editing practices through digital ‘corrections’ to their faces and bodies. The implications of these ever-finer capacities for predictive classificatory processes are essential for understanding how life feels under the gaze of the data industry, and how inequalities and exclusions are made, automated and remade in contemporary datafied lives.

item.title: Does Immersive Journalism Erode News Objectivity? Effects of Immersion on Audience Emotional Engagement and Objectivity Perception
item.dc:creator: Qi Zhou, Zongya Li
item.description:
Digital Journalism · Qi Zhou, Zongya Li

Topics: Journalism, Journalistic practice, Digital journalism, Media effects

Immersive journalism’s potential to foster empathy and engagement has been widely highlighted. However, its impact on the core journalistic norm of objectivity remains critically underexplored. Drawing on a value perception framework, this study examines how immersive news affects enjoyment, alertness, and perceived active objectivity in risk communication. Two between-subjects experiments compared MR-enhanced news with 2D news and high- with low-immersion MR news. Results show that immersion consistently increased enjoyment but reduced alertness. However, the studies did not provide consistent evidence that immersion directly enhances or erodes perceived active objectivity. Instead, more robust pattern emerged through indirect pathways: enjoyment was negatively associated with perceived active objectivity, whereas alertness was positively associated with it. Exploratory moderation analysis further suggests that spatial distance may shape these affective pathways. This study advances a novel value perception framework to digital journalism and demonstrates the interplay effect of immersive strategies and audience characteristics in journalism persuasion.

item.title: Deconstructing the MeToo Movement and the Blue Wave in the 2018 House Elections
item.dc:creator: Lucas Shen
item.description:
Computational Communication Research · Lucas Shen

Topics: MeToo movement, Social movements, Election campaigns, Political participation

At the peak of the #MeToo movement in 2018 is the historical performance of women candidates in the 2018 midterm elections. I examine three ways in which the movement could have an electoral impact using geocoded #MeToo tweets that text analyses show engage core movement discourse and figures, and that geographically predict individual attitudes. I find no credible evidence that the movement increased Democratic vote shares or turnout. Instead, I find that in districts with a stronger movement, Democratic women are more likely to challenge their co-partisan male incumbents, a pattern absent in the Republican Party and in 2016. Hence, the more likely channel is the rise of new Democratic women through a weakening of party norms against same-party challenges.

item.title: FOMO in Sub-Saharan African AI Hype: The Quest for a Decolonized AI Adoption Framework
item.dc:creator: Danford Zirugo, Bruce Mutsvairo
item.description:
Media and Communication · Danford Zirugo, Bruce Mutsvairo

Topics: Artificial intelligence in journalism, Journalism studies, Generative AI, Journalistic practice

Based on an abductive analysis of 54 opinion, editorial, and analytical articles published between 2019 and 2025 in nine English-speaking Sub-Saharan African countries, this study examines negotiation of the place of AI within journalism. Conceptualizing AI hype as a form of metajournalistic discourse, the study finds that discussions about AI in journalism in Sub-Saharan Africa are driven by a fear of missing out and a call for a decolonial approach to the technology’s adoption in a way sensitive to the region’s context.

item.title: Moral Archivists and Agents of Accountability: Typologies of Advocacy Journalism in Local Indonesian Media's Coverage of the Kanjuruhan Tragedy
item.dc:creator: Reza Safitri, Dicky Wahyudi, Ainun Qisthi Rosyidah, Ranee Tuta
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Reza Safitri, Dicky Wahyudi, Ainun Qisthi Rosyidah, Ranee Tuta

Topics: Advocacy journalism, Local media, Journalistic practice, Journalistic roles

This study examines how local media implemented advocacy journalism in their coverage of the Kanjuruhan Tragedy, an event that killed 135 people and triggered prolonged collective trauma in Malang, Indonesia. Using a qualitative approach, the study analyzed 160 news articles and conducted in-depth interviews with journalists and editors from four local media outlets. The findings identify six typologies of advocacy journalism that are not isolated but interconnected, forming a dynamic spectrum of practices. Segmented Advocacy emerges as the dominant form through the direct representation of victims’ voices, often integrated with Emotional Advocacy to build public empathy. Meanwhile, Woven Advocacy and Counter-Frame Advocacy demonstrate strategic critiques that range from implicit to explicit challenges to state narratives. Emerging new typologies and Community Alliance further indicate the expansion of advocacy into cultural, spiritual, and collaborative engagement with civil society. The findings also reveal that institutional pressures and journalist polarization dynamics shape advocacy practices. These findings offer an empirically grounded perspective on advocacy journalism in the Global South, where local media act as moral archivists and agents of accountability sustaining collective memory and justice.

item.title: Harmful YouTube Video Detection: A Taxonomy of Online Harm and MLLMs as Alternative Annotators
item.dc:creator: Wonjeong Jo, Miki Wesołowska, Magdalena Wojcieszak
item.description:
Computational Communication Research · Wonjeong Jo, Miki Wesołowska, Magdalena Wojcieszak

Topics: Content moderation, Large Language Models, Digital platforms, Misinformation

Video platforms, used by billions globally, are criticized for exposing users to harmful content. Yet, detecting online harm remains challenging due to inconsistent approaches to what constitutes harm and limitations of human annotation. We address both challenges. Theoretically, we integrate and expand existing taxonomies and platform guidelines to multimodal contexts and develop a comprehensive taxonomy for online harm. We categorize online harm on video platforms into six content-based categories: Information, Hate and harassment, Addictive, Clickbait, Sexual, and Physical harms. Methodologically, we propose and systematically test multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as alternative annotators of harmful videos. We curate a dataset of 19,422 potentially harmful YouTube videos and annotate them using GPT-4-Turbo, non-trained crowdworkers, and trained annotators. We discuss the potential applications of MLLMs in platform content moderation and social science research, particularly in contexts where they perform comparably to human annotators in binary and multi-label classification tasks.

item.title: Does the TikTok Feed Lean Right? Exposure to Political Content Among Non-Partisan Users in Germany
item.dc:creator: Jasper Tjaden, Johannes Wolfgram, Aaron Philipp, Sarah Weissmann, Licia Bobzien, Ulrich Köhler, Roland Verwiebe
item.description:
Political Communication · Jasper Tjaden, Johannes Wolfgram, Aaron Philipp, Sarah Weissmann, Licia Bobzien, Ulrich Köhler, Roland Verwiebe

Topics: TikTok, Political content exposure, Algorithmic curation, Political polarization

Populist parties are gaining popularity among young voters in many Western democracies. Young voters increasingly obtain news online through social media websites. TikTok has quickly ascended to become one of the most popular platforms globally. We evaluate exposure disparities regarding political parties by measuring the extent to which parties enter non-partisan users’ feeds. By implementing a sock puppet audit using 78 automated users, we can hold individual user behaviour constant – the main mechanisms through which platform algorithms curate user feeds. We collect data in Germany ahead of the three regional elections in 2024 and the federal election in 2025 (N= 561.000 videos). Overall, political content constitutes 4-10% of user feeds in our sample. When non-partisan users encounter (unsolicited) political content, it is more likely to feature videos posted by or supportive of the far-right, populist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party than moderate parties. Further evidence on mechanisms explaining this right-wing visibility advantage points to the importance of multiplier networks and content virality.

item.title: “They Don’t Understand What it Means to be Poor”: How Representation, Relevance, and Relatability Shape the News Experience of Marginalised Young Adults
item.dc:creator: James Dennis
item.description:
Journalism Studies · James Dennis

Topics: News avoidance, Journalism, Social media, Media representation

There are significant concerns about young adults from low socioeconomic backgrounds becoming disengaged from the news. Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with participants aged 18–25 in England, this study examines how social inequality shapes how young adults experience news. Interviewees avoid legacy news media, citing a lack of representation, as stories about them and their communities are omitted from coverage. Where relevant topics are included, they feel that the reporting masks the complexity of how an issue impacts marginalised communities. Crucially, however, this group are not consistent news avoiders but remains engaged with news found on social platforms, accessing perspectives that resonate with their lived experience. This often comes from non-traditional actors who draw on new forms of journalistic storytelling. This paper argues that relatability—understood as a felt sense of proximity to news based on shared communicative norms, cultural experiences, and perceived social relevance—is crucial to understanding this population's news experience. By analysing relatability alongside representation and relevance, the study demonstrates how the interviewees’ lived experience of inequality shapes their relationship to news, both in its content and form. The paper offers practical recommendations for how inclusive storytelling and support for creator journalists can better serve this population.

item.title: Claiming sociodigital futures? Knowledge practices and their consequences
item.dc:creator: Susan Halford, Kirsten F. Cater, Sabine Hauert, Rasheed Hussain, Daniel McQuillan, Weiru Liu
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Susan Halford, Kirsten F. Cater, Sabine Hauert, Rasheed Hussain, Daniel McQuillan, Weiru Liu

Topics: Sociotechnical imaginaries, Digital media, Knowledge practices, Sociology of expectations

There is currently intense and widespread speculation about the implications of digital technologies for future societies, despite a wealth of evidence that past claims to predict how technology will shape the future have usually failed. Nonetheless, it is now well established that claims to knowledge about how emerging technologies will shape future worlds are performative, exercising powerful effects on the futures they claim to describe. Building on the Sociology of Expectations and work on Sociotechnical Imaginaries, this paper turns attention to the ontological and epistemological ‘nuts’ and ‘bolts’ of claims about digital technologies, social life and the future. We ask: how are these entities and the relations between them constituted and given traction as knowledge practices? Specifically, we explore the practices used by major future-claiming institutional actors in a selection of published documents. We find a strikingly coherent ontological performance of the relations between ‘the digital’, ‘the social’ and ‘the future’ and the circulation of (what comes to count as) knowledge across these institutions. Indeed, what is striking is the re-purposability of these knowledge practices despite the distinctive institutional interests in play. These knowledge practices offer a limited grasp on the futures that are currently in the making. Moreover, they enable the persistence of a latent set of assumptions which are powerful in limiting consideration of critical questions about the future.

item.title: From Facebook to front page: the influence of the Gilets Jaunes’ social media on local press language and framing
item.dc:creator: Davide Morselli, Maite Beramendi, Olivier Fillieule
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Davide Morselli, Maite Beramendi, Olivier Fillieule

Topics: Social media activism, Media framing, Journalism, Social movements

This article examines how social media discussions within a protest movement intersect with local news coverage, focusing on the French Gilets Jaunes in the Var department. We hypothesize that journalistic language may progressively align with activists’ semantic universe, thereby contributing to the diffusion of movement claims and terminology. We analyze activists’ Facebook discussions and reporting by the regional daily Var-Matin between 2018 and 2021. Study 1 combines qualitative analysis of reciprocal mentions between Facebook groups and press articles to document mechanisms of interdependence. It shows that local journalists routinely relied on Facebook as a source of information about the movement’s activities and claims, using activists’ online discussions both to anticipate protest events and to contextualize them. Study 2 applies word embeddings to measure semantic proximity between activist and journalistic discourse over time. Results reveal a selective and time-structured semantic convergence consistent with journalists’ sustained exposure to activists’ internal communication. Although Facebook discussions gradually shifted away from some initial claims, local press coverage repeatedly mobilized these founding frames whenever the movement re-entered the news agenda. At the local level, these findings refine the protest paradigm by showing that coverage emphasized protesters’ motivations.

item.title: Whose voices and which effects? A scoping review of migration and social media effects
item.dc:creator: Aleksandra Lazić, Maryam Khaleghipour, Jörg Matthes
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Aleksandra Lazić, Maryam Khaleghipour, Jörg Matthes

Topics: Media effects, Social media, Migration, Differential susceptibility to media effects

Social media plays a central role in shaping migration experiences and public perceptions of migration. However, despite growing research activity, no systematic overview exists on how social media effects are examined across host and migrant populations. This scoping review synthesizes 65 empirical studies on social media effects in the context of migration published between 2020 and 2025. Guided by the differential susceptibility to media effects model, the analysis focuses on content types, sample characteristics, the conceptualization of social media, effect types, and mediating and moderating factors. The findings reveal two largely disconnected strands of research: quantitative, host-focused studies that emphasize negative attitudinal effects, and qualitative, migrant-centered studies that focus on empowerment. Framing effects, platform affordances, producer perspectives, and individual, structural, and social factors remain largely neglected. Overall, the review highlights the need for integrative research that bridges the perspectives of both hosts and migrants and pays greater attention to how migrants themselves perceive, interpret, and respond to social media portrayals and migration-related content.

item.title: Communication strategies and barriers in friends’ mental health conversations on college campuses
item.dc:creator: Aurora Occa, Kelly G. McAninch, Diane B. Francis, Anita Silwal, Hayley M Stahl, Anne Amegbeha Amissah
item.description:
Communication Monographs · Aurora Occa, Kelly G. McAninch, Diane B. Francis, Anita Silwal, Hayley M Stahl, Anne Amegbeha Amissah

Topics: Mental health, College students, Interpersonal communication, Social support

Mental health challenges among college students are common yet difficult to identify and address. Friends often serve as the first line of support, making mental health conversations a critical but understudied intervention avenue. Research has emphasized disclosure over how friends offer support, engage with struggling peers, or handle emotional and relational complexities. These interactions is less studied. We conducted 10 focus groups (N = 68) to examine strategies friends use to navigate mental health conversations and identify facilitating and hindering factors. Participants identified signs of distress, created safe spaces, used direct and indirect strategies to foster conversation, attended to timing, and prioritized protection. Individual, relational, contextual, and societal factors shaped these conversations. We discuss conceptual and practical implications and propose future research.

item.title: Perceiving the News as Toxic: A Longitudinal, Cross-National Analysis of Negative News Evaluations in Flanders and Ireland
item.dc:creator: Pauljan Truyens, Cassandra Craig, Eirini Evangelia Psychari, Ike Picone, John O’Sullivan, Paul McNamara
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Pauljan Truyens, Cassandra Craig, Eirini Evangelia Psychari, Ike Picone, John O’Sullivan, Paul McNamara

Topics: News avoidance, News consumption, Fake news, Longitudinal study

In today’s media environment, where information overload, negativity, and news fatigue are increasingly common, news can feel toxic. Yet little research examines how users perceive this toxicity and adjust their news practices in response. This study addresses that gap through a repeated cross-sectional analysis of Flanders and Ireland. Drawing on DNR-data from 2017-2025 and latent class analysis, we identify three archetypal news repertoires: Panoramic, Limited, and Traditional. Our findings reveal a shift toward limited repertoires, particularly among younger and less socioeconomically advantaged groups, while panoramic repertoires have become rarer, and traditional repertoires have remained stable. These shifts are associated with negative news attitudes, including distrust, avoidance, disinterest, fake news concerns and perceived fake news exposure. The cross-national comparison highlights sharper transitions in Flanders, whereas Irish users retained higher engagement, though early disengagement emerged. By linking negative attitudes or evaluations with changes in repertoires, we contribute to audience research and underscore the need to reconsider the journalism-audience relationship as disengagement is no longer marginal but increasingly mainstream. From a user perspective, repertoire narrowing may be understood as a coping response, although it risks deepening informational inequalities.

item.title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
item.dc:creator: Sacha Altay, Sebastián Valenzuela, Philip N. Howard
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Sacha Altay, Sebastián Valenzuela, Philip N. Howard

Topics: Misinformation, Expert opinion, Information environment, Fake news

How much do experts on the information environment agree about the scale, spread, and effects of misinformation? We drew on three annual waves of the International Panel on the Information Environment expert survey to examine agreement with seven popular claims about misinformation (2023: N = 262; 2024: N = 413; 2025: N = 442; spanning 76 countries). Agreement varied widely across statements and was stable across waves. About 60% of experts agreed that falsehoods spread faster than the truth and that misinformation is widespread. About half agreed that misinformation has a substantial influence on behavior and that people readily believe what they see online; about 40% agreed that more people have become misinformed over time; and only 25% agreed that misinformation is primarily a social media problem. The surveys also revealed a persistent divide between experts who saw misinformation as widespread and consequential and those more skeptical, with sharpest disagreement on its behavioral impact and increase over time. In 2025, some experts distinguished between misperception prevalence and misinformation severity. Overall agreement varied by respondent background: agreement was higher among experts on developing countries than those on developed countries, higher among STEM researchers than social scientists, and lower among political scientists than communication scholars. Expert consensus on misinformation is partial, varies across claims and experts, and is shaped by geography and discipline.

item.title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
item.dc:creator: Linda Li, Helen Margetts
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Linda Li, Helen Margetts

Topics: Social bots, Social media activism, Digital activism, Computational text analysis

Social bots are an increasingly prominent presence in online protest discourse. We adapt the discursive opportunity structure (DOS) framework for digital protest, refining its dimensions of visibility, resonance and legitimacy to account for platform-mediated discourse and automated activity. Applying the refined framework through computer-assisted content analysis of bot activity in two major protests – Black Lives Matter (BLM) and Extinction Rebellion (XR) – we move beyond treating bots as a monolithic or uniformly disruptive force, identifying competing pro- and counter-protest strategies distributed differently across the three dimensions. In BLM, pro-protest bot content concentrates on cultural resonance, whereas counter-bot content targets legitimacy; in XR, pro-protest bots are used to build legitimacy and participatory visibility, whereas counter-bots more often work to downplay the movement’s salience. The framework’s granularity discriminates between movement types in ways coarser accounts of ‘political bots’ cannot, showing that understanding contemporary movements requires attending to how automated activity is deployed within their discourse.

item.title: Social Media Platform Repertoires in Everyday Life: Measuring Social Media Use With Passive Metering
item.dc:creator: Moreno Mancosu, Mario Quaranta, Fabio Torreggiani
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Moreno Mancosu, Mario Quaranta, Fabio Torreggiani

Topics: Social media use, Smartphone use, Digital trace data, Facebook

Social media platforms structure the ways in which billions of citizens access information. Nevertheless, to assess social media time use, most research relies on limited data sources, such as self-reported survey measures or behavioral data from single platforms or convenience samples. Using 6 weeks of passive metering of smartphone and computer activity from a quota sample of Italian adults (18–70, n = 1,457), this study provides a behaviorally measured account of platform-specific social media use across the adult population. We quantify time allocation across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Twitter/X and examine how use varies by sociodemographic factors. Results show that Facebook and YouTube dominate everyday social media time, accounting for nearly three-quarters of consumption, while Instagram attracts comparable average time from a narrower user base, and TikTok shows concentrated usage among younger adopters. Twitter/X occupies a marginal niche. Use is overwhelmingly app-based (>90%), a pattern that browser-based measurement cannot capture. Age is the strongest demographic predictor: Gen Z concentrates attention on Instagram and TikTok, while older cohorts favor Facebook; YouTube shows weak demographic patterning. Gender and education are consistent secondary predictors: women devote more time to Facebook, Instagram, and social media overall, and higher education is associated with lower aggregate use and a smaller share on Facebook and TikTok. Employment and income show null effects. Together, these behavioral, cross-platform figures provide a more accurate basis for weighting platforms by their actual audiences than self-reported or single-platform evidence allows.

item.title: Seeing Is Believing? Most People Struggle to Detect AI-Generated Images
item.dc:creator: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Frederik Hjorth, Yevgeniy Golovchenko, Rebecca Adler‐Nissen, Anja Bechmann, Arjen van Dalen, SARA BINZER HOBOLT, Claes H. de Vreese
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Mads Fuglsang Hove, Frederik Hjorth, Yevgeniy Golovchenko, Rebecca Adler‐Nissen, Anja Bechmann, Arjen van Dalen, SARA BINZER HOBOLT, Claes H. de Vreese

Topics: AI-generated content, Generative AI, Misinformation, Information credibility

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) dramatically lowers the costs of creating high-quality, realistic images, allowing a wider range of actors to create and distribute such content on, for instance, social media. A core concern is that easy-to-use generative AI tools can be misused for manipulation through misinformation and microtargeted persuasive material. However, we still need more contextual nuance to a fundamental question: To what degree can people discern photorealistic AI-generated images from authentic images? In a preregistered survey experiment, we find that, on average, people are not substantially better than chance at discerning AI-generated images from authentic images, regardless of the context of the image. While younger people, highly analytical-thinking individuals, and experienced users of generative AI have better discernment abilities, no demographic group other than young individuals (<25) performs substantially better than chance. Contrary to our expectation, we do not find that people’s confidence in their discernment abilities varies depending on the context of the image. As generative AI technology likely advances and the realism of AI-generated images continues to improve, these findings are concerning, as people already struggle to discern between AI-generated and authentic images, even in an experiment where they have been primed and are assessing images of relatively low quality.

item.title: Algorithms of Injustice: An Ethnographic Content Analysis of Black Youth’s Experiences with Racial Trauma Online
item.dc:creator: Amanda M. McLeroy, Tiera Tanksley
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Amanda M. McLeroy, Tiera Tanksley

Topics: Adolescent mental health, Social media algorithms, Algorithmic curation, Mental health

This study explores the pervasive presence of racially traumatic content (RTC) on social media and its profound impact on the mental well-being of Black youth. Utilizing ethnographic content analysis and grounded in critical race technology theory (CRTT), the research identifies key manifestations of RTC, including Black death, digital harassment, deepfakes, and war content. Social media’s algorithmic structures amplify RTC, perpetuating systemic anti-Black racism while exposing Black youth to vicarious trauma, anxiety, and depression. Despite these challenges, social media platforms also provide spaces for activism and community-building. Black youth use these digital arenas to engage in social justice narratives, find solidarity, and develop coping strategies. The findings emphasize the critical roles of educators and counselors in mitigating the adverse effects of RTC by fostering media literacy, digital resilience, and culturally responsive mental health support. This research contributes to evidence-based interventions aimed at empowering Black youth to navigate digital spaces safely, advocate for systemic change, and thrive in an equitable and inclusive online environment.

item.title: Webs of Ainu Mosir: Indigenous Creative Networks on YouTube
item.dc:creator: Xanat Vargas Meza, Takumi Yokoyama, Chieko Nishimura, Ryohei Nishida, Ochiai Yoichi
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Xanat Vargas Meza, Takumi Yokoyama, Chieko Nishimura, Ryohei Nishida, Ochiai Yoichi

Topics: Social networks, Social media, Online communities, Digital media

The Ainu are Indigenous people living primarily in Japan. As they have recently adopted social media, and network-based analyses of First Nations cultural manifestations are uncommon, this study drew on Indigenous and social network frameworks to examine creative networks in the virtual Mosir (the world as viewed by the Ainu). Our objective was to clarify the types of collaborators, their cooperation patterns and relationships relevant to producing Ainu-related YouTube videos. Three YouTube lists of 428 videos were utilised in this study. Publicly available data were downloaded using a YouTube Application Programming Interface (API). The videos were watched and classified, including anonymised data on collaborators. The relationships of the collaborators were quantified and mapped, network measurements were calculated and collaborator clusters were examined. The most frequent types of collaborators were individuals and communities. We also observed that individuals moderately affected network clustering ( p = .002). Furthermore, individuals were somewhat correlated with the average number of ties ( p = .004) and the bridging of clusters through betweenness ( p = .006), with Japanese male celebrities and Ainu people, particularly Ainu women, showing high centrality. As Indigenous rights advance internationally, the virtual Mosir shows how crucial it is for First Nations to participate in multimedia production processes, particularly if such productions are available on social media. Indigenous network frameworks were highly compatible with network analysis, allowing for a more comprehensive overview of Indigenous production processes. This can enhance the multiple knowledges of First Nations, while fostering accountability and reciprocity of their allies.

item.title: Careful Dis/Connection: Bringing Digital (Inter)Dependent Relations Out From the Shadows of Autonomy
item.dc:creator: Sara Van Bruyssel
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Sara Van Bruyssel

Topics: Digital well-being, Digital media, Well-being, Privacy

Although always-on connectivity affords autonomy, it also creates dependencies on digital devices. Digital disconnection has emerged as a countermovement, with people seeking ‘authentic’ offline reconnection under the discourse of (self-)care. Yet, a pertinent question is whether certain care relations are contingent on digital dependencies between people and, despite being perceived as burdensome, should therefore not be broken through disconnection. Drawing on feminist ethics of care, which understands care as all the work that maintains everyday life, this article examines how care and digital dis/connection practices shape each other. Empirically, it draws on ethnographic fieldwork with 20 adults and analyses three vignettes through a relational framework that follows care occurring in, through and away from digital devices. The findings show that digital well-being is shaped less by individual media use than by the care relations that digital technologies sustain. Experiences of digital dis/connection reveal how connectivity is embedded in often invisible responsibilities, dependencies, and forms of care. Rather than locating digital tensions in technologies themselves, the analysis suggests that such tensions expose underlying challenges in how care is organised, valued, and distributed. In response, the article develops the framework of careful dis/connection to evaluate digital practices according to how they sustain, redistribute, and make visible the care on which everyday life depends.

item.title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
item.dc:creator: Samuel Hardman Taylor, David M. Markowitz
item.description:
Social Media + Society · Samuel Hardman Taylor, David M. Markowitz

Topics: Social media algorithms, Longitudinal study, Computational methods, Social media use

Perceptions of how algorithms curate content are integral to how people use social media and its effects. Building on the algorithm responsiveness process, we explore whether perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR) was associated with the message cues of algorithmically curated content. We coupled longitudinal data from a 7-day, twice-daily diary survey with computational digital traces from Twitter (now X) to operationalize algorithmic message characteristics and to understand the antecedents and outcomes of PAR ( N = 10,337 tweets). Results suggested that message cues from algorithmic content in social feeds (i.e., closeness, popularity, valence, and format) were associated with perceived message personalization, but message personalization was the only message characteristic associated with PAR. PAR predicted feeling more connected to others on Twitter, along with message-level factors: closeness to the poster and message personalization. This work contributes to the algorithm responsiveness process, demonstrating that characteristics of algorithmically curated messages predict how individuals experience algorithms.

item.title: Press freedom in a post-authoritarian context: evolving challenges for Bangladeshi journalists after Sheikh Hasina
item.dc:creator: Manwar Hossain, Mahbubul Haque Bhuiyan, Muhammad Saurav Rahman, Md Saddam Hossain
item.description:
Journalism · Manwar Hossain, Mahbubul Haque Bhuiyan, Muhammad Saurav Rahman, Md Saddam Hossain

Topics: Press freedom, Journalism, Political communication, Journalistic practice

Authoritarian constraints on press freedom manifest across diverse political contexts, from typical illiberal democracies to flawed democracies. While substantial scholarship examines journalistic challenges under authoritarian rule, the dynamics of press freedom in recent post-authoritarian transitions remain underexplored. Drawing on in-depth interviews with journalists from Bangladesh, this article investigates how press freedom evolves in these settings. Findings show that an authoritarian regime change does not guarantee press freedom or journalist safety. The study makes three theoretical contributions. First, ownership structures and political pressures from authoritarian periods persist after regime transitions. Second, control over the press may shift from predictable, top-down tools (laws and state agencies) to more scattered, bottom-up forces, such as street intimidation and social media harassment. Finally, the press-power relationship is often renegotiated rather than automatically liberalized following authoritarian collapse.

item.title: When Populism? Consistent and Opportunistic Populist Communication in the 2022 Brazilian Presidential Elections
item.dc:creator: Gustavo Luiz Venturelli, Paolo Ricci, Guilherme Tiengo, Raphaela Velho
item.description:
Political Communication · Gustavo Luiz Venturelli, Paolo Ricci, Guilherme Tiengo, Raphaela Velho

Topics: Populism, Political communication, Election campaigns, Computational methods

When do presidential candidates use populist communication, and does its prevalence vary across policy domains? We address these questions using an original dataset of 11,885 tweets from nine Brazilian presidential candidates during the 2022 elections. Drawing on the ideational approach, we operationalize populist discourse as the co-occurrence of people-centrism and anti-elitism, measured with fine-tuned BERT-based classifiers, and classify policy domains with the Comparative Agendas Project framework. Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity across candidates, challenging expectations that populist communication uniformly intensifies during campaigns or systematically varies across policy domains according to ideology. Rather than increasing uniformly during the campaign, populist appeals escalate strategically for some candidates as elections approach, while remaining stable for others throughout the electoral year. We propose a typology distinguishing opportunistic from consistent populists. Across policy domains, government operations serve as a baseline facilitating populist framing. Left-wing candidates increase populist rhetoric in labor/employment, consistent with issue ownership expectations, but right-wing candidates reduce populist appeals in their traditionally owned domains of law and crime and civil rights, contrary to expectations. Overall, we show that populism is neither a universal campaign imperative nor a content-neutral communication style, but a flexible discursive frame shaped by candidate strategy, electoral context, and policy content.

item.title: Skewed toward uniformity? Investigating algorithmic stereotyping and amplification in AI-generated images
item.dc:creator: Daniela Mahl, Lars Guenther
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · Daniela Mahl, Lars Guenther

Topics: Artificial intelligence, Generative AI, Media representation, Algorithmic curation

As text-to-image generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes visual communication, concerns are growing about its role in reproducing social stereotypes. While recent algorithm auditing studies have advanced our understanding of stereotypical AI-generated imagery, they have largely focused on a narrow set of stereotypes – primarily gender and race – overlooking more nuanced forms. Addressing this gap, our study adopts a case-sensitive approach that conceptualizes stereotypes as multi-layered phenomena composed of multiple, context-specific indicators. Applying the Draw-a-Scientist Test framework, we analyzed stereotypical representations of scientists in images generated by DALL·E 3 and examined potential amplification by benchmarking against Google Images. Specifically, we compared 16 stereotype indicators across six stereotype subjects. Using Latent Class Analysis, we identified six classes reflecting distinct patterns of stereotypical depiction. Our findings show that DALL·E not only produces highly stereotypical portrayals of scientists but also amplifies these patterns compared to Google Images. Both image sources lack adequate visual references for disciplines beyond the traditional laboratory context – a pattern we interpret as epistemic narrowing, whereby diverse forms of knowledge production are reduced to a uniform, laboratory-based representation of science. We conclude by discussing potential drivers of epistemic narrowing, the broader implications of algorithmic visibility, and mitigation strategies.

item.title: From constituencies to audiences: lessons from Brazil about audience analytics in representative politics
item.dc:creator: André K. Rodarte
item.description:
Information, Communication & Society · André K. Rodarte

Topics: Political communication, Audience perception, Mediatization, Social media use

The pursuit of audiences is a key driver of the mediatization of politics, yet it remains unclear how parliamentarians carry out this task. Drawing on interviews with members of Brazil’s Congress, this study investigates how politicians incorporate audience analytics into their communication strategies. It introduces a conceptual framework of audience perception – distinguishing among loyalists, followers, and audience reservoirs – to explain how politicians interpret digital publics. Findings reveal that parliamentarians’ perceptions of their audiences differ from their perceptions of electoral bases. Their follower base undergoes context collapse, disembedding audiences from their social context. Digital media re-embed these constituencies in platform contexts, wherein parliamentarians believe they must become always-on content producers, perform authenticity, and engage in information cycles. These findings reveal that audience analytics incentivize a sales orientation in parliamentary communication, distorting representation by recasting audiences as targets of influence rather than publics to whom politicians are accountable.

item.title: Immersion Matters: Virtual Reality Influences Personal and Systemic Bias Outcomes
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth S. Noland, Christopher R. Agnew, Margo J. Monteith
item.description:
Media Psychology · Elisabeth S. Noland, Christopher R. Agnew, Margo J. Monteith

Topics: Virtual reality, Racial bias, Empathy, Media effects

Social psychological research has used traditional empathy-inducing strategies (e.g. reading, listening to, or watching narratives) to heighten recognition of and motivation to combat personal and systemic bias. We investigated whether a non-embodied 360° virtual reality (VR) experience increased recognition of and motivation to combat both personal and systemic racial bias and examined empathy as an underlying mechanism. Non-Black undergraduates in the United States (N = 313) were randomly assigned to (a) a non-embodied immersive 360° VR experience depicting racial discrimination, (b) an audio-only version of the same experience, or (c) a race-unrelated audio (control). VR exposure (vs. audio-only and control) heightened recognition of systemic bias, motivation to combat both systemic and personal bias, and perceptions of racism in isolated incidents. Emotional empathy, but not cognitive empathy, was a significant mediator. In contrast, the audio-only condition did not differ from the VR or control condition on personal and systemic bias outcomes or recognition of racism. These findings highlight the theoretical and practical value of non-embodied 360° immersive VR as a tool for combating personal and systemic bias.

item.title: Algorithmic News Selection Under News Avoidance: Assessing News Values on Chinese Tiktok (Douyin)
item.dc:creator: Jinhui Li, Wen Shi
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Jinhui Li, Wen Shi

Topics: News avoidance, Algorithmic curation, Social media algorithms, News values

This study explores how recommendation algorithms on Douyin respond to users’ growing disengagement from news by shaping the visibility of news content. Adopting an agent-based testing (ABT) approach, we conducted a 2 (intentional news avoidance: 0% vs. 100%) × 2 (unintentional news avoidance: 50% vs. 100%) between-subject experiment to simulate distinct user behaviors and capture large-scale data from news-related videos. Findings indicated that two avoidance behavioral patterns result in contrasting algorithmic outcomes which reinforce or weaken certain news values such as prominence, uniqueness, timeliness, and influence. A significant interaction effect further reveals that the influence of intentional news avoidance on the news values of influence diminishes as users’ preference for non-news content increases, whereas its influence on uniqueness becomes stronger. These findings show that recommender systems adapt to user disengagement by reprioritizing content, highlighting algorithmic curation as a socio-technical process that shapes attention amid selective news exposure.

item.title: Soft Power from the Outside, Career Choice from the Inside: Understanding Job Attractions of Chinese Media Expats in Thailand
item.dc:creator: Tucker Wang-Hai
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Tucker Wang-Hai

Topics: Journalism, Professional identity, Media systems, Journalistic practice

China’s global media expansion is often interpreted as a state-led soft power strategy. Yet little is known about how individual journalists enact this expansion while working overseas for Chinese media organizations. Taking Thailand as an empirical case, this article examines how Chinese journalists assigned to overseas postings come to view their roles as a worthwhile career decision. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Thailand and in-depth interviews with Chinese expat journalists, it argues that alignment with state goals emerges not from ideological commitment, but from personal motivations, career timing, and everyday practical reasoning. The article draws on Bourdieu’s concept of illusio to conceptualize this process as a socially grounded belief that the pursuit is worth investment. Journalists accept overseas postings insofar as these roles make sense within their own trajectories, at once professionally viable and personally meaningful. The findings complement state-centric models of media expansion and offers a framework for understanding journalists’ on-the-ground motivations amid broader transformations in global journalism.

item.title: The Many Notions of Audience Engagement: A Scoping Review
item.dc:creator: Bernadette Uth
item.description:
Journalism Studies · Bernadette Uth

Topics: Audience engagement, Journalism studies, Engaged journalism, News media

In recent years, “audience engagement” and “engaged journalism” have emerged as buzzwords in journalism studies. Audience engagement is regularly discussed as a potential remedy for declining trust in journalism and its precarious financial situation. Over the past two decades, journalism studies have thus extensively analyzed the concept, resulting in a vast body of literature on engagement. However, this has created definitional confusion around audience engagement, with numerous definitions, interpretations and characteristics of the concept discussed in existing scholarship. By conducting a systematic scoping review of 174 peer-reviewed journal articles on audience engagement, this study sheds closer light on the existing research on engagement, offers an overview on theoretical and empirical conceptualizations, and examines goals and challenges associated with engagement. The review highlights how audience engagement is examined and conceptualized in journalism scholarship, and identifies key directions for future research.
